questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A steel tube of length $1.00 \text{ m}$ is struck at one end. A person with an ear close to the opposite end hears the sound of the blow twice: once travelling through the body of the tube and once through the air inside the tube. Determine the time gap between the two hearings. (Take the speed of sound in air as $340 \text{ m/s}$ and in steel as $5200 \text{ m/s}$.)
questions.solution:
Time taken by sound to travel through air is $t_1 = \dfrac{L}{v_a} = \dfrac{1}{340} \text{ s}$

Time taken by sound to travel through steel is $t_2 = \dfrac{L}{v_s} = \dfrac{1}{5200} \text{ s}$

The time gap between the two hearings is $\Delta t = t_1 - t_2$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{340} - \dfrac{1}{5200}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{5200 - 340}{340 \times 5200}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{4860}{1768000} \text{ s}$

$\Delta t \approx 2.75 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s} = 2.75 \text{ ms}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A man stands in front of a large wall at a distance of $50.0 \text{ m}$ and claps his hands at regular intervals. Initially, the interval is large. He progressively reduces the interval, fixing it at a value where the echo of a clap merges with the subsequent clap. If he claps $10$ times during every $3$ seconds, determine the velocity of sound in air.
questions.solution:
Let the distance of the man from the wall be $d = 50.0 \text{ m}$.

The sound of the clap travels to the wall and reflects back to the man. The total distance traveled by the sound to hear the echo is $2d = 100 \text{ m}$.

Let the velocity of sound be $v$. The time taken for the echo to reach the man is:
$t = \dfrac{2d}{v}$

The man progressively reduces the time interval between claps until the echo of a clap merges exactly with the subsequent clap. This means the time taken for the echo to return is exactly equal to the time interval between two successive claps.

The man claps $10$ times during every $3$ seconds, which implies the frequency of clapping is $f = \dfrac{10}{3} \text{ Hz}$.

The time interval between successive claps is:
$T = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{3}{10} = 0.3 \text{ s}$

Equating the echo time to the clap interval:
$\dfrac{2d}{v} = T$

$\dfrac{100}{v} = 0.3$

$v = \dfrac{100}{0.3} = 333.33 \text{ m/s}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the velocity of sound is $333 \text{ m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the minimum and maximum wavelengths of sound in water within the audible range ($20$–$20000 \text{ Hz}$) for an average human ear. The speed of sound in water is $1450 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The relation between speed, frequency, and wavelength is given by $v = f \lambda$.

The minimum wavelength corresponds to the maximum frequency:

$\lambda_{min} = \dfrac{v}{f_{max}}$

$\lambda_{min} = \dfrac{1450}{20000} = 0.0725 \text{ m} = 7.25 \text{ cm}$

The maximum wavelength corresponds to the minimum frequency:

$\lambda_{max} = \dfrac{v}{f_{min}}$

$\lambda_{max} = \dfrac{1450}{20} = 72.5 \text{ m}$

The minimum and maximum wavelengths are $7.25 \text{ cm}$ and $72.5 \text{ m}$ respectively.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person is able to hear sound waves within the frequency range of $20 \text{ Hz}$ to $20 \text{ kHz}$. Determine the minimum and maximum wavelengths of sound audible to the person. Assume the speed of sound is $360 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Given, speed of sound, $v = 360 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Minimum frequency, $f_{\min} = 20 \text{ Hz}$

Maximum frequency, $f_{\max} = 20 \text{ kHz} = 20000 \text{ Hz}$

The relation between speed, frequency, and wavelength is given by $v = f \lambda \Rightarrow \lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$

For minimum wavelength, frequency must be maximum:

$\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{v}{f_{\max}} = \dfrac{360}{20000} = 18 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} = 18 \text{ mm}$

For maximum wavelength, frequency must be minimum:

$\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{v}{f_{\min}} = \dfrac{360}{20} = 18 \text{ m}$

Thus, the minimum and maximum wavelengths are $18 \text{ mm}$ and $18 \text{ m}$ respectively.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Sound is primarily transmitted in the forward direction when its wavelength is significantly smaller than the speaker's diameter. Determine the frequency at which the sound's wavelength is one tenth of the diameter of a loudspeaker whose diameter is $20 \text{ cm}$. Assume the speed of sound is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Given diameter of the loudspeaker, $D = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$

Wavelength of the sound, $\lambda = \dfrac{D}{10} = 0.02 \text{ m}$

Speed of sound, $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Using the relation $v = f \lambda$, the frequency $f$ is given by:

$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$

$f = \dfrac{340}{0.02} = 17000 \text{ Hz}$

$f = 17 \text{ kHz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Sound waves from a loudspeaker propagate nearly uniformly in all directions when the sound's wavelength is significantly greater than the loudspeaker's diameter. Compute the frequency at which the wavelength of sound in air equals ten times the speaker's diameter, given a diameter of $20 \text{ cm}$. Take the speed of sound as $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Given diameter of the loudspeaker, $D = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$.

The wavelength of sound is ten times the speaker's diameter:

$\lambda = 10 \times D = 10 \times 0.2 = 2 \text{ m}$

The speed of sound is given as $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Using the relation between speed, frequency, and wavelength, $v = f \lambda$, we get:

$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{340}{2} = 170 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: During a spiritual gathering, the devotees chant HARE-RAM HARE-RAM. The sound is amplified by a loudspeaker and returns after reflecting from a building situated $80 \text{ m}$ away from the gathering. Determine the maximum time interval that can be maintained between one HARE-RAM and the following HARE-RAM such that the echo does not disturb a listener seated in the gathering. The speed of sound in air is $320 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The time taken for the sound to travel to the building and reflect back to the listener is given by $t = \dfrac{2d}{v}$

Substituting the given values:

$t = \dfrac{2 \times 80}{320} = 0.5 \text{ s}$

For the echo not to disturb the listener, the reflected sound of the first chant must coincide with the chanting of the second one. If the time interval between the chants is greater than $0.5 \text{ s}$, the echo will be heard separately, causing a disturbance.

Thus, the maximum time interval that can be maintained between consecutive chants is $0.5 \text{ s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A travelling sound wave is described by the equation $y = 6.0 \sin(600 t - 1.8 x)$, with $y$ measured in $10^{-5} \text{ m}$, $t$ in second, and $x$ in metre. Determine the ratio of the displacement amplitude of the particles to the wavelength of the wave.
questions.solution:
The given equation of the travelling sound wave is $y = 6.0 \sin(600 t - 1.8 x)$.

Comparing this with the standard wave equation $y = A \sin(\omega t - k x)$, we get:
Displacement amplitude, $A = 6.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$
Angular wave number, $k = 1.8 \text{ rad/m}$

The wavelength $\lambda$ of the wave is given by:
$\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = \dfrac{2\pi}{1.8} = \dfrac{\pi}{0.9} \text{ m}$

The ratio of the displacement amplitude to the wavelength is:
$\dfrac{A}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{-5}}{\dfrac{\pi}{0.9}} = \dfrac{5.4 \times 10^{-5}}{\pi}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$, we get:
$\dfrac{A}{\lambda} = \dfrac{5.4 \times 10^{-5}}{3.14} \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A travelling sound wave is described by the equation $y = 6.0 \sin(600 t - 1.8 x)$, with $y$ measured in $10^{-5} \text{ m}$, $t$ in second, and $x$ in metre. Determine the ratio of the velocity amplitude of the particles to the wave speed.
questions.solution:
The given equation of the wave is $y = 6.0 \times 10^{-5} \sin(600 t - 1.8 x)$.

Comparing with the standard wave equation $y = A \sin(\omega t - k x)$, we get:
$A = 6.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$
$\omega = 600 \text{ rad/s}$
$k = 1.8 \text{ m}^{-1}$

The velocity amplitude of the particles is given by $v_m = A \omega$.

The wave speed is given by $v = \dfrac{\omega}{k}$.

The ratio of the velocity amplitude of the particles to the wave speed is:
$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{v_m}{v} = \dfrac{A \omega}{\omega / k} = A k$

Substituting the values:
$\text{Ratio} = (6.0 \times 10^{-5}) \times 1.8 = 10.8 \times 10^{-5} = 1.08 \times 10^{-4} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sound wave having a frequency of $100 \text{ Hz}$ is travelling in air. The speed of sound in air is $350 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. By how much does the phase change at a given point in $2.5 \text{ ms}$?
questions.solution:
The phase of a wave at a fixed position $x$ as a function of time $t$ is given by $\phi = \omega t - kx + \phi_0$.

The change in phase at a given point over a time interval $\Delta t$ is given by:

$\Delta \phi = \omega \Delta t = 2\pi f \Delta t$

Given frequency $f = 100 \text{ Hz}$ and time interval $\Delta t = 2.5 \text{ ms} = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$.

Substituting the values:

$\Delta \phi = 2\pi \times 100 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-3}$

$\Delta \phi = 2\pi \times 0.25$

$\Delta \phi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: To detect tumours in soft tissues, ultrasonic waves with a frequency of $4.5 \text{ MHz}$ are utilized. The speed of sound is $1.5 \text{ km s}^{-1}$ in tissue and $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ in air. Determine the wavelength of these ultrasonic waves in air and in tissue, respectively.
questions.solution:
Given frequency, $f = 4.5 \text{ MHz} = 4.5 \times 10^{6} \text{ Hz}$

Speed of sound in air, $v_{a} = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Speed of sound in tissue, $v_{t} = 1.5 \text{ km s}^{-1} = 1500 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The wavelength of the ultrasonic waves in air is given by:

$\lambda_{a} = \dfrac{v_{a}}{f} = \dfrac{340}{4.5 \times 10^{6}} \text{ m}$

$\lambda_{a} \approx 75.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m} \approx 7.6 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$

The wavelength of the ultrasonic waves in tissue is given by:

$\lambda_{t} = \dfrac{v_{t}}{f} = \dfrac{1500}{4.5 \times 10^{6}} \text{ m}$

$\lambda_{t} \approx 333.3 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m} \approx 3.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$

Thus, the wavelengths in air and tissue are $7.6 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$ and $3.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$ respectively.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sound wave having a frequency of $100 \text{ Hz}$ is travelling in air. The speed of sound in air is $350 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. What is the phase difference at a given instant between two points separated by a distance of $10.0 \text{ cm}$ along the direction of propagation?
questions.solution:
Given frequency $f = 100 \text{ Hz}$ and speed of sound $v = 350 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The wavelength of the sound wave is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{350}{100} = 3.5 \text{ m}$

The phase difference $\Delta \phi$ between two points separated by a distance $\Delta x$ is:

$\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$

Given $\Delta x = 10.0 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$. Substituting the values:

$\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{3.5} \times 0.1 = \dfrac{0.2\pi}{3.5} = \dfrac{2\pi}{35}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two point sources of sound are separated by $10 \text{ cm}$. They vibrate in phase, generating waves with a wavelength of $5.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the phase difference between the two waves arriving at a point located $20 \text{ cm}$ from one source on the line connecting the sources.
questions.solution:
Let the two sources be $S_1$ and $S_2$ with a separation $d = 10 \text{ cm}$.

The point $P$ is located on the line passing through $S_1$ and $S_2$ at a distance of $20 \text{ cm}$ from one of the sources. Since $20 \text{ cm} > 10 \text{ cm}$, the point $P$ lies outside the segment $S_1 S_2$.

For any point on the line outside the segment connecting the two sources, the path difference $\Delta x$ between the waves from the two sources is exactly equal to the distance between the sources.

$\Delta x = |S_1 P - S_2 P| = d = 10 \text{ cm}$

The phase difference $\Delta \phi$ is given by the relation:

$\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$

Substituting $\lambda = 5.0 \text{ cm}$ and $\Delta x = 10 \text{ cm}$:

$\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{5.0} \times 10 = 4\pi$

A phase difference of $4\pi$ is an integer multiple of $2\pi$, which is equivalent to a phase difference of $0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two point sources of sound are separated by $10 \text{ cm}$. They vibrate in phase, generating waves with a wavelength of $5.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the phase difference between the two waves arriving at a point located $20 \text{ cm}$ from one source on the perpendicular bisector of the line connecting the sources.
questions.solution:
Let the two point sources be $S_1$ and $S_2$, and the observation point be $P$.

The point $P$ is located on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining the two sources. By the geometric property of a perpendicular bisector, any point on it is equidistant from both the sources.

Given that the distance of point $P$ from one source is $20 \text{ cm}$, its distance from the other source must also be $20 \text{ cm}$.

$S_1P = 20 \text{ cm}$

$S_2P = 20 \text{ cm}$

The path difference $\Delta x$ between the two waves reaching point $P$ is:

$\Delta x = S_1P - S_2P = 20 \text{ cm} - 20 \text{ cm} = 0$

The phase difference $\Delta \phi$ is related to the path difference by the formula:

$\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$

Substituting $\Delta x = 0$:

$\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{5.0} \times 0 = 0$

Since the sources vibrate in phase, the initial phase difference is also zero. Thus, the total phase difference at point $P$ is $0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the speed of sound in oxygen using the following data. At STP ($T = 273 \text{ K}$ and $p = 1.0 \times 10^5 \text{ N m}^{-2}$), the mass of $22.4$ litre of oxygen is $32 \text{ g}$. The molar heat capacity of oxygen is $C_V = 2.5 R$ at constant volume and $C_p = 3.5 R$ at constant pressure.
questions.solution:
The ratio of specific heats is $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_V} = \dfrac{3.5 R}{2.5 R} = 1.4$

The density of oxygen at STP is $\rho = \dfrac{M}{V} = \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}}{22.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3} = \dfrac{10}{7} \text{ kg m}^{-3}$

The speed of sound in a gas is given by Laplace's formula $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma p}{\rho}}$

Substituting the given values:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{1.4 \times 1.0 \times 10^5}{10/7}}$

$v = \sqrt{1.4 \times 0.7 \times 10^5}$

$v = \sqrt{0.98 \times 10^5} = \sqrt{98000}$

$v \approx 313 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: On a winter day, a student in the laboratory measures the speed of sound to be $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ when the room temperature is $17^\circ \text{C}$. Determine the speed that will be measured by another student performing the same experiment on a day when the room temperature is $32^\circ \text{C}$.
questions.solution:
The speed of sound in a gas is directly proportional to the square root of its absolute temperature, $v \propto \sqrt{T}$.

Given $v_1 = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $T_1 = 17^\circ \text{C} = 17 + 273 = 290 \text{ K}$.

We need to find the speed $v_2$ at $T_2 = 32^\circ \text{C} = 32 + 273 = 305 \text{ K}$.

Using the relation $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}$:

$v_2 = 340 \sqrt{\dfrac{305}{290}}$

$v_2 = 340 \sqrt{\dfrac{61}{58}}$

$v_2 \approx 340 \times 1.0255 \approx 348.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Rounding to the nearest integer gives $349 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the temperature at which the speed of sound is twice its value at $0^\circ \text{C}$.
questions.solution:
The speed of sound in a gas is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma R T}{M}}$, which implies $v \propto \sqrt{T}$, where $T$ is the absolute temperature.

Let $v_1$ be the speed at $T_1 = 0^\circ \text{C} = 273 \text{ K}$ and $v_2$ be the speed at temperature $T_2$.

Given $v_2 = 2v_1$, we have:

$\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}} = 2$

$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 4$

$T_2 = 4T_1$

Substituting $T_1 = 273 \text{ K}$:

$T_2 = 4 \times 273 \text{ K} = 1092 \text{ K}$

Converting to Celsius:

$T_2 = 1092 - 273 = 819^\circ \text{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a space of width $d$, the absolute temperature of air linearly increases from $T_1$ to $T_2$. Determine the time taken by a sound wave to travel through this region in terms of $T_1$, $T_2$, $d$, and the speed $v$ of sound at $273 \text{ K}$. Evaluate this time for $T_1 = 280 \text{ K}$, $T_2 = 310 \text{ K}$, $d = 33 \text{ m}$, and $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The speed of sound at an absolute temperature $T$ is given by:

$v_T = v \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{273}}$

Since the temperature increases linearly with distance $x$ from $0$ to $d$, the temperature at a distance $x$ is:

$T(x) = T_1 + \dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{d} x$

Differentiating with respect to $x$ gives:

$dT = \dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{d} dx \Rightarrow dx = \dfrac{d}{T_2 - T_1} dT$

The time taken by the sound wave to travel a small distance $dx$ is $dt = \dfrac{dx}{v_T}$. Integrating from $x = 0$ to $x = d$ (which corresponds to $T = T_1$ to $T = T_2$):

$t = \int_{T_1}^{T_2} \dfrac{d}{T_2 - T_1} \dfrac{\sqrt{273}}{v \sqrt{T}} dT$

$t = \dfrac{d \sqrt{273}}{v (T_2 - T_1)} \int_{T_1}^{T_2} T^{-1/2} dT$

$t = \dfrac{d \sqrt{273}}{v (T_2 - T_1)} \left[ 2\sqrt{T} \right]_{T_1}^{T_2}$

$t = \dfrac{2d \sqrt{273}}{v (T_2 - T_1)} (\sqrt{T_2} - \sqrt{T_1})$

Using the identity $T_2 - T_1 = (\sqrt{T_2} - \sqrt{T_1})(\sqrt{T_2} + \sqrt{T_1})$, we get:

$t = \dfrac{2d \sqrt{273}}{v (\sqrt{T_1} + \sqrt{T_2})}$

Substituting the given values $d = 33 \text{ m}$, $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, $T_1 = 280 \text{ K}$, and $T_2 = 310 \text{ K}$:

$t = \dfrac{2 \times 33 \times \sqrt{273}}{330 (\sqrt{280} + \sqrt{310})}$

$t = \dfrac{66 \times 16.52}{330 (16.73 + 17.61)}$

$t = \dfrac{1090.32}{330 \times 34.34} \approx 0.096 \text{ s} = 96 \text{ ms}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the change in volume of $1.0$ litre of kerosene upon being subjected to an additional pressure of $2.0 \times 10^5 \text{ N m}^{-2}$, given the following data: density of kerosene $= 800 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and speed of sound in kerosene $= 1330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The speed of sound in a liquid is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{B}{\rho}}$, where $B$ is the bulk modulus and $\rho$ is the density.

Squaring both sides, the bulk modulus is $B = \rho v^{2}$.

The bulk modulus is also defined as $B = \dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta V / V}$, where $\Delta P$ is the change in pressure, $V$ is the initial volume, and $\Delta V$ is the change in volume.

Equating the two expressions for $B$:

$\dfrac{\Delta P \cdot V}{\Delta V} = \rho v^{2}$

Rearranging for $\Delta V$:

$\Delta V = \dfrac{\Delta P \cdot V}{\rho v^{2}}$

Substituting the given values $\Delta P = 2.0 \times 10^{5} \text{ N m}^{-2}$, $V = 1.0 \text{ litre} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}^{3}$, $\rho = 800 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, and $v = 1330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$\Delta V = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{5} \times 10^{-3}}{800 \times (1330)^{2}}$

$\Delta V = \dfrac{200}{800 \times 1768900}$

$\Delta V = \dfrac{1}{4 \times 1768900} = \dfrac{1}{7075600} \text{ m}^{3}$

$\Delta V \approx 1.413 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^{3}$

Converting to $\text{cm}^{3}$:

$\Delta V = 1.413 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{6} \text{ cm}^{3} \approx 0.14 \text{ cm}^{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the bulk modulus of air using the given data for a sound wave of wavelength $35 \text{ cm}$ travelling in air. The pressure at a specific point fluctuates between $(1.0 \times 10^5 \pm 14) \text{ Pa}$, and the particles of the air undergo simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of $5.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
The pressure amplitude $\Delta P_m$ of a sound wave is related to the bulk modulus $B$, the wave number $k$, and the displacement amplitude $A$ by the relation:

$\Delta P_m = B k A$

The wave number $k$ is given by $k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$. Substituting this into the equation gives:

$\Delta P_m = B \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\right) A$

Rearranging for the bulk modulus $B$:

$B = \dfrac{\Delta P_m \lambda}{2\pi A}$

Given the values:
Pressure amplitude, $\Delta P_m = 14 \text{ Pa}$
Wavelength, $\lambda = 35 \text{ cm} = 0.35 \text{ m}$
Displacement amplitude, $A = 5.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$

Substituting these values into the formula:

$B = \dfrac{14 \times 0.35}{2 \times \pi \times 5.5 \times 10^{-6}}$

Using $\pi \approx \dfrac{22}{7}$:

$B = \dfrac{4.9}{11 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10^{-6}}$

$B = \dfrac{4.9 \times 7}{242 \times 10^{-6}}$

$B = \dfrac{34.3}{242} \times 10^6$

$B \approx 1.41 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$

Rounding to two significant figures, we get $1.4 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source of sound operates at $2.0 \text{ kHz}$ and $20 \text{ W}$, radiating sound uniformly in all directions. Given that the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the density of air is $1.2 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, what is the intensity at a distance of $6.0 \text{ m}$ from the source?
questions.solution:
The intensity of sound at a distance $r$ from a point source radiating uniformly in all directions is given by the power divided by the surface area of a sphere of radius $r$.

$I = \dfrac{P}{4 \pi r^2}$

Given:
Power of the source, $P = 20 \text{ W}$
Distance, $r = 6.0 \text{ m}$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$I = \dfrac{20}{4 \pi (6.0)^2}$

$I = \dfrac{20}{4 \pi \times 36}$

$I = \dfrac{5}{36 \pi} \text{ W m}^{-2}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:

$I \approx \dfrac{5}{113.04} \text{ W m}^{-2}$

$I \approx 0.0442 \text{ W m}^{-2}$

$I \approx 44 \text{ mW m}^{-2}$

The frequency, speed of sound, and density of air are extra information not required for this calculation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source of sound operates at $2.0 \text{ kHz}$ and $20 \text{ W}$, radiating sound uniformly in all directions. Given that the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the density of air is $1.2 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, what is the pressure amplitude at a distance of $6.0 \text{ m}$ from the source?
questions.solution:
Intensity of sound at a distance $r$ from a point source is given by

$I = \dfrac{P}{4 \pi r^2}$

The relation between intensity and pressure amplitude $p_m$ is

$I = \dfrac{p_m^2}{2 \rho v}$

Equating the two expressions for intensity:

$\dfrac{P}{4 \pi r^2} = \dfrac{p_m^2}{2 \rho v}$

$p_m = \sqrt{\dfrac{P \rho v}{2 \pi r^2}}$

Substituting the given values $P = 20 \text{ W}$, $\rho = 1.2 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $r = 6.0 \text{ m}$:

$p_m = \sqrt{\dfrac{20 \times 1.2 \times 340}{2 \pi \times (6.0)^2}}$

$p_m = \sqrt{\dfrac{8160}{72 \pi}}$

$p_m = \sqrt{\dfrac{340}{3 \pi}}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:

$p_m \approx \sqrt{36.07} \approx 6.0 \text{ Pa}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source of sound operates at $2.0 \text{ kHz}$ and $20 \text{ W}$, radiating sound uniformly in all directions. Given that the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the density of air is $1.2 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, what is the displacement amplitude at a distance of $6.0 \text{ m}$ from the source?
questions.solution:
The intensity $I$ of a sound wave radiating uniformly in all directions from a point source is given by:

$I = \dfrac{P}{4 \pi r^2}$

The intensity is also related to the displacement amplitude $s_0$ of the sound wave by the formula:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v \omega^2 s_0^2$

Since $\omega = 2 \pi f$, we can write:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v (2 \pi f)^2 s_0^2 = 2 \pi^2 \rho v f^2 s_0^2$

Equating the two expressions for intensity:

$2 \pi^2 \rho v f^2 s_0^2 = \dfrac{P}{4 \pi r^2}$

$s_0^2 = \dfrac{P}{8 \pi^3 r^2 \rho v f^2}$

$s_0 = \dfrac{1}{2 \pi r f} \sqrt{\dfrac{P}{2 \pi \rho v}}$

Substituting the given values ($P = 20 \text{ W}$, $r = 6.0 \text{ m}$, $\rho = 1.2 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$, $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, $f = 2000 \text{ Hz}$):

$s_0 = \dfrac{1}{2 \pi (6.0) (2000)} \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{2 \pi (1.2) (340)}}$

$s_0 = \dfrac{1}{24000 \pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{816 \pi}} = \dfrac{1}{24000 \pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{204 \pi}}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.1416$:

$s_0 \approx \dfrac{1}{75398} \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{640.89}} \approx \dfrac{0.0883}{75398} \approx 1.17 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$

Rounding to the nearest given option, we get $1.2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When the intensity of sound is doubled, by how many decibels does the sound level increase?
questions.solution:
The sound level in decibels is given by the formula:

$L = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I}{I_0} \right)$

When the intensity is doubled, the new intensity is $I' = 2I$. The new sound level is:

$L' = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{2I}{I_0} \right)$

The increase in sound level is:

$\Delta L = L' - L = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{2I}{I_0} \right) - 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I}{I_0} \right)$

$\Delta L = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{2I / I_0}{I / I_0} \right) = 10 \log_{10}(2)$

Substituting the value of $\log_{10}(2) \approx 0.3010$:

$\Delta L = 10 \times 0.3010 = 3.01 \text{ dB}$

The sound level increases by approximately $3 \text{ dB}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At a distance of $5.0 \text{ m}$ from a point source, the intensity of sound is $1.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ W m}^{-2}$. Determine the intensity at a distance of $25 \text{ m}$ from the source.
questions.solution:
For a point source, the intensity of sound $I$ is inversely proportional to the square of the distance $r$ from the source.

$I \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{I_2}{I_1} = \left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2$

Given $I_1 = 1.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ W m}^{-2}$, $r_1 = 5.0 \text{ m}$, and $r_2 = 25 \text{ m}$.

$\dfrac{I_2}{1.0 \times 10^{-8}} = \left(\dfrac{5.0}{25}\right)^2$

$\dfrac{I_2}{1.0 \times 10^{-8}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{25}$

$I_2 = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-8}}{25} = 0.04 \times 10^{-8} \text{ W m}^{-2}$

$I_2 = 4.0 \times 10^{-10} \text{ W m}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At a distance of $5.0 \text{ m}$ from a point source, the sound level is $40 \text{ dB}$. Determine the sound level at a point located $50 \text{ m}$ away from the source.
questions.solution:
The intensity of sound from a point source varies inversely with the square of the distance:

$I \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$

The ratio of intensities at distances $r_1 = 5.0 \text{ m}$ and $r_2 = 50 \text{ m}$ is:

$\dfrac{I_2}{I_1} = \left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{5.0}{50}\right)^2 = 10^{-2}$

The sound level in decibels is given by $\beta = 10 \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$. The difference in sound levels is:

$\beta_2 - \beta_1 = 10 \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I_2}{I_1}\right)$

Substituting the given values:

$\beta_2 - 40 = 10 \log_{10}(10^{-2})$

$\beta_2 - 40 = -20$

$\beta_2 = 20 \text{ dB}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Sound with an intensity exceeding $120 \text{ dB}$ appears painful to a person. A small speaker delivers $2.0 \text{ W}$ of audio output. Determine how close the person can get to the speaker without hurting his ears.
questions.solution:
The intensity level $\beta$ in decibels is given by $\beta = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I}{I_0} \right)$, where $I_0 = 10^{-12} \text{ W/m}^2$.

Substituting $\beta = 120 \text{ dB}$:

$120 = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} \right)$

$\log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} \right) = 12$

$I = 10^{12} \times 10^{-12} = 1 \text{ W/m}^2$

The intensity $I$ at a distance $r$ from a point source of power $P$ is given by $I = \dfrac{P}{4 \pi r^2}$.

Substituting $I = 1 \text{ W/m}^2$ and $P = 2.0 \text{ W}$:

$1 = \dfrac{2.0}{4 \pi r^2}$

$r^2 = \dfrac{1}{2 \pi}$

$r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \text{ m}$

$r \approx \dfrac{1}{2.506} \text{ m} \approx 0.399 \text{ m}$

$r \approx 40 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the sound level within a room is raised from $50 \text{ dB}$ to $60 \text{ dB}$, by what factor does the pressure amplitude increase?
questions.solution:
The sound level in decibels is given by $\beta = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I}{I_0} \right)$

The difference in sound level is $\Delta \beta = 60 - 50 = 10 \text{ dB}$

$\beta_2 - \beta_1 = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I_2}{I_1} \right)$

$10 = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I_2}{I_1} \right)$

$\dfrac{I_2}{I_1} = 10$

The intensity of a sound wave is directly proportional to the square of its pressure amplitude, $I \propto P_0^2$

$\left( \dfrac{P_{02}}{P_{01}} \right)^2 = \dfrac{I_2}{I_1} = 10$

$\dfrac{P_{02}}{P_{01}} = \sqrt{10}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the absence of the teacher, the noise level in a classroom containing $50$ students is $50 \text{ dB}$. Assuming that each student, on average, emits the same sound energy per second, determine the noise level if the number of students increases to $100$.
questions.solution:
Let the sound intensity produced by one student be $I_{s}$ and the reference intensity be $I_{0}$.

The total intensity produced by $50$ students is $I_{1} = 50I_{s}$.

The noise level is given by $L_{1} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I_{1}}{I_{0}} \right) = 50 \text{ dB}$.

When the number of students increases to $100$, the new intensity is $I_{2} = 100I_{s}$.

The new noise level is $L_{2} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I_{2}}{I_{0}} \right)$.

The difference in noise levels is $L_{2} - L_{1} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{I_{2}}{I_{1}} \right)$.

Substituting the values, $L_{2} - 50 = 10 \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{100I_{s}}{50I_{s}} \right) = 10 \log_{10}(2)$.

Since $\log_{10}(2) \approx 0.301$, we get $L_{2} - 50 = 10 \times 0.301 \approx 3$.

$L_{2} = 53 \text{ dB}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: During Quincke's experiment, the detected sound transitions from a maximum to a minimum as the sliding tube is shifted by a distance of $2.50 \text{ cm}$. Determine the frequency of the sound, given that the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
In Quincke's tube experiment, when the sliding tube is moved by a distance $x$, the path difference between the two interfering sound waves changes by $2x$.

For the sound intensity to transition from a maximum to a minimum, the change in path difference must be $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$.

Equating the two expressions for the change in path difference:

$2x = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda = 4x$

Given $x = 2.50 \text{ cm} = 0.025 \text{ m}$, the wavelength is:

$\lambda = 4 \times 0.025 = 0.1 \text{ m}$

The frequency of the sound wave is given by $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$.

Substituting $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $\lambda = 0.1 \text{ m}$:

$f = \dfrac{340}{0.1} = 3400 \text{ Hz} = 3.4 \text{ kHz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In Quincke's experiment, the sound intensity exhibits a minimum value $I$ at a specific position. When the sliding tube is pulled out by a distance of $16.5 \text{ mm}$, the intensity rises to a maximum of $9 I$. Taking the speed of sound in air as $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the frequency of the sound source.
questions.solution:
In Quincke's tube experiment, when the sliding tube is pulled out by a distance $\Delta x$, the path difference between the two interfering sound waves changes by $\Delta p = 2\Delta x$.

The change in path difference required to transition from a minimum intensity to the adjacent maximum intensity is $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$.

Equating the two expressions for the change in path difference:

$2\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$

$\Rightarrow \lambda = 4\Delta x$

Given $\Delta x = 16.5 \text{ mm} = 16.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, the wavelength is:

$\lambda = 4 \times 16.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} = 66 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

The frequency of the sound source is given by:

$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$

Substituting $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$f = \dfrac{330}{66 \times 10^{-3}} = 5000 \text{ Hz} = 5.0 \text{ kHz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In Quincke's experiment, the sound intensity exhibits a minimum value $I$ at a specific position. When the sliding tube is pulled out by a distance of $16.5 \text{ mm}$, the intensity rises to a maximum of $9 I$. Taking the speed of sound in air as $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the ratio of the amplitudes of the two waves arriving at the detector, assuming this ratio remains largely unchanged between the positions of minimum and maximum intensity.
questions.solution:
The minimum intensity is given as $I_{min} = I$ and the maximum intensity is $I_{max} = 9I$.

The intensity of sound is proportional to the square of its amplitude. For two waves of amplitudes $A_1$ and $A_2$, the maximum and minimum intensities are given by:

$I_{max} = k(A_1 + A_2)^2$

$I_{min} = k(A_1 - A_2)^2$

Taking the ratio of the maximum to minimum intensity:

$\dfrac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \dfrac{(A_1 + A_2)^2}{(A_1 - A_2)^2} = \dfrac{9I}{I} = 9$

Taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{A_1 + A_2}{A_1 - A_2} = 3$

Cross-multiplying yields:

$A_1 + A_2 = 3A_1 - 3A_2$

$4A_2 = 2A_1$

$\dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = 2$

The ratio of the amplitudes of the two waves is $2$. The data regarding the displacement of the tube and the speed of sound is extraneous for finding this ratio.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Driven by the same amplifier system, two audio speakers are positioned some distance apart. A person is seated $6.0 \text{ m}$ from one speaker and $6.4 \text{ m}$ from the other. If the sound signal is continuously varied from $500 \text{ Hz}$ to $5000 \text{ Hz}$, determine the frequencies that produce destructive interference at the listener's location. The speed of sound in air is $320 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
options: $600 \text{ Hz}$, $1400 \text{ Hz}$, $2200 \text{ Hz}$, $3000 \text{ Hz}$, $3800 \text{ Hz}$ and $4600 \text{ Hz}$
$800 \text{ Hz}$, $1600 \text{ Hz}$, $2400 \text{ Hz}$, $3200 \text{ Hz}$, $4000 \text{ Hz}$ and $4800 \text{ Hz}$
$1000 \text{ Hz}$, $2000 \text{ Hz}$, $3000 \text{ Hz}$, $4000 \text{ Hz}$ and $5000 \text{ Hz}$
$1200 \text{ Hz}$, $2000 \text{ Hz}$, $2800 \text{ Hz}$, $3600 \text{ Hz}$ and $4400 \text{ Hz}$
questions.solution:
The path difference between the sound waves reaching the listener is $\Delta x = 6.4 \text{ m} - 6.0 \text{ m} = 0.4 \text{ m}$.

For destructive interference, the path difference must be an odd multiple of half the wavelength:

$\Delta x = (2n - 1) \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$

Using the relation $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$, we get:

$\Delta x = (2n - 1) \dfrac{v}{2f}$

Substituting the given values $\Delta x = 0.4 \text{ m}$ and $v = 320 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$0.4 = (2n - 1) \dfrac{320}{2f}$

$f = \dfrac{160}{0.4} (2n - 1) = 400(2n - 1) \text{ Hz}$

Substituting integer values for $n$:

For $n = 1$, $f = 400 \text{ Hz}$

For $n = 2$, $f = 1200 \text{ Hz}$

For $n = 3$, $f = 2000 \text{ Hz}$

For $n = 4$, $f = 2800 \text{ Hz}$

For $n = 5$, $f = 3600 \text{ Hz}$

For $n = 6$, $f = 4400 \text{ Hz}$

For $n = 7$, $f = 5200 \text{ Hz}$

Since the frequency varies from $500 \text{ Hz}$ to $5000 \text{ Hz}$, the frequencies producing destructive interference are $1200 \text{ Hz}$, $2000 \text{ Hz}$, $2800 \text{ Hz}$, $3600 \text{ Hz}$, and $4400 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sound source $S$ and a detector $D$ are located at some distance from each other. A large cardboard is placed near the detector, perpendicular to the line $SD$, as shown in the figure. The cardboard is gradually moved away, and it is observed that the intensity varies from a maximum to a minimum when the board is displaced by a distance of $20 \text{ cm}$. Determine the frequency of the emitted sound. The velocity of sound in air is $336 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Let the distance between the detector $D$ and the cardboard be $x$.

The sound waves reaching the detector consist of the direct wave from the source $S$ and the reflected wave from the cardboard. The reflected wave travels an additional distance from the detector to the cardboard and back. Thus, the path difference between the direct and reflected waves is:
$\Delta p = 2x$

When the cardboard is displaced by a distance $\Delta x = 20 \text{ cm}$, the new path difference becomes $2(x + \Delta x)$. The change in the path difference is:
$\Delta p' = 2\Delta x = 2 \times 20 \text{ cm} = 40 \text{ cm}$

For the intensity at the detector to vary from a maximum (constructive interference) to an adjacent minimum (destructive interference), the change in path difference must be equal to half of the wavelength $\left(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\right)$.

Equating the two expressions for the change in path difference:
$\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 40 \text{ cm}$
$\Rightarrow \lambda = 80 \text{ cm} = 0.8 \text{ m}$

The frequency of the emitted sound $f$ can be calculated using the wave speed equation $v = f\lambda$:
$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{336 \text{ m s}^{-1}}{0.8 \text{ m}} = 420 \text{ Hz}$

questions.q: A source $S$ and a detector $D$ are separated by a distance $d$. As shown in the figure, a large cardboard is positioned at a distance $\sqrt{2}d$ from the source and the detector. The source emits a wave with a wavelength of $d/2$, which reaches the detector after reflecting off the cardboard. This reflected wave is observed to be in phase with the direct wave arriving from the source. Determine the minimum distance the cardboard must be shifted away such that the reflected wave becomes out of phase with the direct wave.
questions.solution:
Path length of the direct wave from $S$ to $D$ is $x_1 = d$.

Path length of the reflected wave is $x_2 = 2\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}d)^2 + \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2} = 2\sqrt{2d^2 + \dfrac{d^2}{4}} = 3d$.

Initial path difference is $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1 = 3d - d = 2d$.

Given wavelength $\lambda = \dfrac{d}{2}$, the path difference is $\Delta x = 4\lambda$. This confirms the waves are initially in phase.

To make the waves out of phase by shifting the cardboard away by a minimum distance, the new path difference must be $\Delta x' = 4.5\lambda = 4.5 \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right) = 2.25d$.

Let the new distance of the cardboard be $y$. The new path length of the reflected wave is $x_2' = 2\sqrt{y^2 + \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2}$.

The new path difference is:

$x_2' - x_1 = 2.25d$

$2\sqrt{y^2 + \dfrac{d^2}{4}} - d = 2.25d$

$2\sqrt{y^2 + \dfrac{d^2}{4}} = 3.25d$

$\sqrt{y^2 + \dfrac{d^2}{4}} = 1.625d$

Squaring both sides:

$y^2 + 0.25d^2 = (1.625)^2 d^2 = 2.640625 d^2$

$y^2 = 2.390625 d^2$

$y = \sqrt{2.390625} d \approx 1.546 d$

The minimum shift required is:

$\Delta y = y - \sqrt{2}d \approx 1.546 d - 1.414 d = 0.132 d \approx 0.13 d$.

Answer: $0.13 d$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two stereo speakers are separated by a distance of $2.40 \text{ m}$. A person stands at a distance of $3.20 \text{ m}$ directly in front of one of the speakers, as shown in the figure. Determine the frequencies in the audible range ($20$–$2000 \text{ Hz}$) for which the listener will hear a minimum sound intensity. The speed of sound in air is $320 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Let the two speakers be $S_1$ and $S_2$, and the listener be at point $P$.

The distance from the first speaker to the listener is:
$L_1 = 3.20 \text{ m}$

The distance from the second speaker to the listener is:
$L_2 = \sqrt{(2.40)^2 + (3.20)^2} = \sqrt{5.76 + 10.24} = \sqrt{16.00} = 4.00 \text{ m}$

The path difference $\Delta x$ between the sound waves reaching the listener is:
$\Delta x = L_2 - L_1 = 4.00 - 3.20 = 0.80 \text{ m}$

For minimum sound intensity (destructive interference), the path difference must be an odd multiple of half the wavelength:
$\Delta x = (2n + 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$, where $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$

Using the relation $v = f\lambda$, we have $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$. Substituting this into the condition for destructive interference:
$\Delta x = (2n + 1)\dfrac{v}{2f}$

Solving for the frequency $f$:
$f = (2n + 1)\dfrac{v}{2\Delta x}$

Given the speed of sound $v = 320 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $\Delta x = 0.80 \text{ m}$:
$f = (2n + 1)\dfrac{320}{2 \times 0.80} = (2n + 1)\dfrac{320}{1.60} = 200(2n + 1) \text{ Hz}$

The listener can hear frequencies in the audible range $20 \text{ Hz} \le f \le 2000 \text{ Hz}$:
$20 \le 200(2n + 1) \le 2000$

Dividing by $200$:
$0.1 \le 2n + 1 \le 10$

Subtracting $1$:
$-0.9 \le 2n \le 9$

Dividing by $2$:
$-0.45 \le n \le 4.5$

Since $n$ must be a non-negative integer, the possible values are $n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$.

Thus, the frequencies for minimum sound intensity are $200(2n + 1) \text{ Hz}$, where $n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$.

questions.q: Two sound sources, $S_1$ and $S_2$, emitting waves of identical wavelength $20.0 \text{ cm}$, are positioned with a separation of $20.0 \text{ cm}$ between them. A detector can move along a line parallel to $S_1 S_2$ and at a distance of $20.0 \text{ cm}$ from it. Initially, the detector lies equidistant from both sources. Assuming the waves emitted by the sources are in phase, determine the minimum distance the detector must be shifted to detect a sound minimum.
questions.solution:
Given wavelength $\lambda = 20.0 \text{ cm}$, distance between sources $d = 20.0 \text{ cm}$, and distance to the line of movement $D = 20.0 \text{ cm}$.

For the first minimum, the path difference must be $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 10.0 \text{ cm}$.

Let the sources be located at $(-10, 0)$ and $(10, 0)$. The detector is initially at $(0, 20)$ and moves to a new position $(x, 20)$.

The distances from the sources to the detector are $S_1 P = \sqrt{(x + 10)^2 + 20^2}$ and $S_2 P = \sqrt{(x - 10)^2 + 20^2}$.

The path difference is $\Delta x = S_1 P - S_2 P = 10$.

$\sqrt{(x + 10)^2 + 400} - \sqrt{(x - 10)^2 + 400} = 10$

$\sqrt{(x + 10)^2 + 400} = 10 + \sqrt{(x - 10)^2 + 400}$

Squaring both sides:

$(x + 10)^2 + 400 = 100 + (x - 10)^2 + 400 + 20 \sqrt{(x - 10)^2 + 400}$

$x^2 + 20x + 500 = x^2 - 20x + 600 + 20 \sqrt{(x - 10)^2 + 400}$

$40x - 100 = 20 \sqrt{(x - 10)^2 + 400}$

Dividing by 20:

$2x - 5 = \sqrt{(x - 10)^2 + 400}$

Squaring both sides again:

$(2x - 5)^2 = (x - 10)^2 + 400$

$4x^2 - 20x + 25 = x^2 - 20x + 100 + 400$

$3x^2 = 475$

$x = \sqrt{\dfrac{475}{3}} \approx \sqrt{158.33} \approx 12.58 \text{ cm}$

Rounding to one decimal place, the minimum distance the detector must be shifted is $12.6 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two speakers $S_1$ and $S_2$, powered by a common amplifier, are situated at $y = 1.0 \text{ m}$ and $y = -1.0 \text{ m}$ as shown in the figure. These speakers vibrate in phase at $600 \text{ Hz}$. A man is standing at a point on the X-axis located at a very large distance from the origin and begins to move parallel to the Y-axis. The speed of sound in air is given as $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. At what angle $\theta$ does the sound intensity decrease to a minimum for the first time?
questions.solution:
The distance between the two speakers is $d = 1.0 - (-1.0) = 2.0 \text{ m}$.

The wavelength of the sound wave is given by:
$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{330}{600} = 0.55 \text{ m}$

For a point at a very large distance, the path difference between the sound waves reaching the man at an angle $\theta$ is $\Delta x = d \sin \theta$.

The sound intensity decreases to a minimum for the first time when the path difference is equal to $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$.

$d \sin \theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$

Substituting the values, we get:
$2.0 \sin \theta = \dfrac{0.55}{2}$

$\sin \theta = \dfrac{0.275}{2.0} = 0.1375$

For small angles, $\sin \theta \approx \theta$ (in radians), so $\theta \approx 0.1375 \text{ rad}$.

Converting to degrees:
$\theta \approx 0.1375 \times \dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi} \approx 7.88^\circ$

Thus, the angle is approximately $7.9^\circ$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two speakers $S_1$ and $S_2$, powered by a common amplifier, are situated at $y = 1.0 \text{ m}$ and $y = -1.0 \text{ m}$ as shown in the figure. These speakers vibrate in phase at $600 \text{ Hz}$. A man is standing at a point on the X-axis located at a very large distance from the origin and begins to move parallel to the Y-axis. The speed of sound in air is given as $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. At what angle $\theta$ will the man experience a maximum of sound intensity for the first time?
questions.solution:
The distance between the two speakers $S_1$ and $S_2$ is $d = 1.0 - (-1.0) = 2.0 \text{ m}$.

The wavelength of the sound wave is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{330}{600} = 0.55 \text{ m}$

For a point at a very large distance from the origin at an angle $\theta$ with the X-axis, the path difference between the sound waves reaching the man from $S_1$ and $S_2$ is:

$\Delta x = d \sin \theta$

The man starts from the X-axis ($\theta = 0^\circ$), where there is a central maximum. As he moves parallel to the Y-axis, he will experience the first maximum of sound intensity when the path difference equals one wavelength ($\lambda$).

$\Delta x = \lambda$

$d \sin \theta = \lambda$

Substituting the values, we get:

$2.0 \sin \theta = 0.55$

$\sin \theta = \dfrac{0.55}{2.0} = 0.275$

We know that $\sin 15^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.259$. Since $0.275$ is slightly greater than $0.259$, the angle $\theta$ must be slightly greater than $15^\circ$.

From the given options, the closest angle is $16^\circ$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two speakers $S_1$ and $S_2$, powered by a common amplifier, are situated at $y = 1.0 \text{ m}$ and $y = -1.0 \text{ m}$ as shown in the figure. These speakers vibrate in phase at $600 \text{ Hz}$. A man is standing at a point on the X-axis located at a very large distance from the origin and begins to move parallel to the Y-axis. The speed of sound in air is given as $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. If he continues walking along the same line past the first maximum, how many additional maxima can he hear?
questions.solution:
The wavelength of the sound wave is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{330}{600} = 0.55 \text{ m}$

The distance between the two speakers $S_1$ and $S_2$ is:

$d = 1.0 - (-1.0) = 2.0 \text{ m}$

For an observer at a very large distance from the origin, the path difference $\Delta x$ at an angle $\theta$ from the X-axis is:

$\Delta x = d \sin \theta$

For a maximum (constructive interference), the path difference must be an integer multiple of the wavelength:

$\Delta x = n\lambda \implies d \sin \theta = n\lambda$

Substituting the values, we get:

$2.0 \sin \theta = n(0.55) \implies \sin \theta = 0.275 n$

Since the maximum value of $\sin \theta$ is $1$ (as $\theta \to 90^\circ$ when the man moves to infinity parallel to the Y-axis):

$0.275 n \le 1 \implies n \le \dfrac{1}{0.275} \approx 3.63$

The possible non-negative integer values for $n$ are $0, 1, 2, 3$.

The man starts at a point on the X-axis, where $\theta = 0^\circ$. This corresponds to the central maximum ($n = 0$).

As he moves parallel to the Y-axis, $\theta$ increases, and he will successively encounter the maxima for $n = 1, 2, 3$.

The first maximum he encounters while walking corresponds to $n = 1$.

If he continues walking past this first maximum, the additional maxima he will hear correspond to $n = 2$ and $n = 3$.

Therefore, he will hear $2$ additional maxima.

questions.q: Three sound sources $S_1$, $S_2$, and $S_3$ of equal intensity are arranged along a straight line such that $S_1 S_2 = S_2 S_3$, as depicted in the figure. At a distant point $P$, the wave arriving from $S_2$ leads the wave from $S_1$ in phase by $120^\circ$. Furthermore, the wave arriving from $S_3$ leads the wave from $S_2$ by $120^\circ$. Determine the resultant intensity of the sound at $P$.
options: The intensity of a single source
Three times the intensity of a single source
Nine times the intensity of a single source
questions.solution:
Let the intensity of each individual sound source be $I_0$, and the corresponding amplitude be $A_0$.

The wave arriving from $S_2$ leads the wave from $S_1$ by $120^\circ$, and the wave from $S_3$ leads the wave from $S_2$ by $120^\circ$. The equations of the three waves arriving at point $P$ can be written as:

$y_1 = A_0 \sin(\omega t)$

$y_2 = A_0 \sin(\omega t + 120^\circ)$

$y_3 = A_0 \sin(\omega t + 240^\circ)$

The resultant displacement at point $P$ is given by the principle of superposition:

$y = y_1 + y_2 + y_3$

$y = A_0 [\sin(\omega t) + \sin(\omega t + 120^\circ) + \sin(\omega t + 240^\circ)]$

Using the trigonometric identity $\sin C + \sin D = 2 \sin\left(\dfrac{C+D}{2}\right) \cos\left(\dfrac{C-D}{2}\right)$ for the last two terms:

$\sin(\omega t + 120^\circ) + \sin(\omega t + 240^\circ) = 2 \sin(\omega t + 180^\circ) \cos(-60^\circ)$

Since $\sin(\omega t + 180^\circ) = -\sin(\omega t)$ and $\cos(-60^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{2}$:

$\sin(\omega t + 120^\circ) + \sin(\omega t + 240^\circ) = 2 (-\sin(\omega t)) \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\sin(\omega t)$

Substituting this back into the equation for $y$:

$y = A_0 [\sin(\omega t) - \sin(\omega t)] = 0$

Since the resultant amplitude is zero, the resultant intensity at point $P$ is also zero.

questions.q: Two coherent narrow slits emitting sound of wavelength $\lambda$ in the same phase are situated parallel to one another with a small separation of $2\lambda$. The sound is detected by sliding a detector along the screen $\Sigma$ positioned at a distance $D (\gg \lambda)$ from the slit $S_1$, as depicted in the figure. Determine the distance $x$ such that the intensity at $P$ matches the intensity at $O$.
questions.solution:
The path difference at point $O$ is given by:

$\Delta x_O = S_1O - S_2O = D - (D - 2\lambda) = 2\lambda$

Since the path difference is an integer multiple of the wavelength, constructive interference occurs at $O$, resulting in maximum intensity.

For the intensity at point $P$ to match the intensity at $O$, constructive interference must also occur at $P$. The path difference at $P$ is:

$\Delta x_P = S_1P - S_2P = \sqrt{D^2 + x^2} - \sqrt{(D - 2\lambda)^2 + x^2}$

As $x$ increases, the path difference decreases from $2\lambda$ towards $0$. The next maximum intensity occurs when the path difference is $\lambda$. Thus, we set:

$\sqrt{D^2 + x^2} - \sqrt{(D - 2\lambda)^2 + x^2} = \lambda$

Let $y = \sqrt{D^2 + x^2}$. The equation becomes:

$y - \sqrt{y^2 - 4D\lambda + 4\lambda^2} = \lambda$

$y - \lambda = \sqrt{y^2 - 4D\lambda + 4\lambda^2}$

Squaring both sides, we get:

$y^2 - 2y\lambda + \lambda^2 = y^2 - 4D\lambda + 4\lambda^2$

$2y\lambda = 4D\lambda - 3\lambda^2$

$y = 2D - 1.5\lambda$

Given that $D \gg \lambda$, we can approximate $y \approx 2D$. Substituting back $y = \sqrt{D^2 + x^2}$:

$\sqrt{D^2 + x^2} = 2D$

Squaring both sides:

$D^2 + x^2 = 4D^2$

$x^2 = 3D^2$

$x = \sqrt{3}D$

Answer: $\sqrt{3} D$

questions.q: Two sources of sound $S_1$ and $S_2$ vibrate at the same frequency and are in phase as shown in the figure. The intensity of sound detected at point $P$ is $I_0$ when both sources are active. If one source is switched off, what will be the intensity at $P$? Consider (a) $\theta = 45^\circ$ and (b) $\theta = 60^\circ$.
questions.solution:
From the given figure, point $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $S_1S_2$, so the path difference is zero ($\\Delta x = 0$).

Let the intensity of each individual source at $P$ be $I'$.

Since the sources are in phase and the path difference is zero, they interfere constructively. The resultant intensity is:

$I_0 = I' + I' + 2\\sqrt{I' I'} \\cos 0^\\circ = 4I'$

If one source is switched off, the intensity at $P$ is solely due to the single remaining source, which is $I'$.

New intensity $= I' = \\dfrac{I_0}{4}$

This result depends only on the path difference being zero and is completely independent of the angle $\\theta$.

questions.q: As shown in the figure, two coherent sources $S_1$ and $S_2$ emit sound of wavelength $\lambda$ in phase. The separation between the sources is $3\lambda$. A circular wire of large radius is placed such that $S_1 S_2$ lies in its plane, with the middle point of $S_1 S_2$ located at the centre of the wire. Determine the angular positions $\theta$ in the first quadrant on the wire at which constructive interference takes place.
questions.solution:
Let the distance between the two coherent sources $S_1$ and $S_2$ be $d = 3\lambda$.

For a point $P$ on the circular wire of large radius at an angular position $\theta$, the rays from $S_1$ and $S_2$ are approximately parallel.

The path difference $\Delta x$ between the waves reaching point $P$ from $S_1$ and $S_2$ is given by:

$\Delta x = d \cos \theta$

Substituting $d = 3\lambda$, we get:

$\Delta x = 3\lambda \cos \theta$

For constructive interference, the path difference must be an integral multiple of the wavelength $\lambda$:

$\Delta x = n\lambda$

Equating the two expressions for path difference:

$3\lambda \cos \theta = n\lambda$

$\Rightarrow \cos \theta = \dfrac{n}{3}$

Since we need the angular positions in the first quadrant, $\theta$ lies in the range $[0^\circ, 90^\circ]$, which implies $0 \le \cos \theta \le 1$.

The possible integer values for $n$ are $0, 1, 2,$ and $3$.

For $n = 3$, $\cos \theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = 0^\circ$

For $n = 2$, $\cos \theta = \dfrac{2}{3} \Rightarrow \theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$

For $n = 1$, $\cos \theta = \dfrac{1}{3} \Rightarrow \theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)$

For $n = 0$, $\cos \theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = 90^\circ$

Thus, the angular positions for constructive interference in the first quadrant are $0^\circ, \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right), \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right), 90^\circ$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the fundamental, first overtone, and second overtone frequencies of an open organ pipe having a length of $20 \text{ cm}$. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
For an open organ pipe, the fundamental frequency is given by $f_1 = \dfrac{v}{2L}$

Substituting the given values, $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $L = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$:

$f_1 = \dfrac{340}{2 \times 0.2} = \dfrac{340}{0.4} = 850 \text{ Hz}$

The first overtone corresponds to the second harmonic, $f_2 = 2f_1$:

$f_2 = 2 \times 850 = 1700 \text{ Hz}$

The second overtone corresponds to the third harmonic, $f_3 = 3f_1$:

$f_3 = 3 \times 850 = 2550 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A closed organ pipe can vibrate with a minimum frequency of $500 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the length of the tube. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The minimum frequency of vibration for a closed organ pipe corresponds to its fundamental frequency, which is given by the formula:

$f = \dfrac{v}{4L}$

Substituting the given values, $f = 500 \text{ Hz}$ and $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$500 = \dfrac{340}{4L}$

$L = \dfrac{340}{4 \times 500}$

$L = \dfrac{340}{2000} = 0.17 \text{ m}$

$L = 17 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a standing wave pattern within a vibrating air column, nodes are formed at a distance of $40 \text{ cm}$. If the speed of sound in air is $328 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the frequency of the source.
questions.solution:
The distance between two consecutive nodes in a standing wave is $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$.

Given that nodes are formed at a distance of $40 \text{ cm}$, we have:

$\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$

$\lambda = 0.8 \text{ m}$

The speed of sound is given as $v = 328 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The frequency of the source is:

$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{328}{0.8} = 410 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a vibrating air column, the distance between a node and the adjacent antinode is $25 \text{ cm}$. If the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the frequency of vibration of the air column.
questions.solution:
The distance between a node and the adjacent antinode is $\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$.

$\dfrac{\lambda}{4} = 25 \text{ cm} = 0.25 \text{ m}$

$\lambda = 4 \times 0.25 \text{ m} = 1 \text{ m}$

The frequency of vibration is given by $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$.

Substituting the given values:

$f = \dfrac{340}{1} = 340 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylindrical metal tube is open at both ends and has a length of $50 \text{ cm}$. Determine the frequencies between $1000 \text{ Hz}$ and $2000 \text{ Hz}$ at which the air column inside the tube can resonate. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
For a tube open at both ends, the resonant frequencies are given by $f_n = \dfrac{nv}{2L}$, where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$

Given $L = 50 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \text{ m}$ and $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, the fundamental frequency is:

$f_1 = \dfrac{340}{2 \times 0.5} = 340 \text{ Hz}$

The possible resonant frequencies are integral multiples of the fundamental frequency:

$f_n = n \times 340 \text{ Hz}$

Calculating the frequencies for different values of $n$:

For $n = 3$, $f_3 = 3 \times 340 = 1020 \text{ Hz}$

For $n = 4$, $f_4 = 4 \times 340 = 1360 \text{ Hz}$

For $n = 5$, $f_5 = 5 \times 340 = 1700 \text{ Hz}$

For $n = 6$, $f_6 = 6 \times 340 = 2040 \text{ Hz}$

The frequencies that lie strictly between $1000 \text{ Hz}$ and $2000 \text{ Hz}$ are $1020 \text{ Hz}$, $1360 \text{ Hz}$, and $1700 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a resonance column experiment, a tuning fork of frequency $400 \text{ Hz}$ is utilized. The first resonance is noticed when the length of the air column is $20.0 \text{ cm}$, while the second resonance occurs when the air column length is $62.0 \text{ cm}$. Find the speed of sound in air.
questions.solution:
Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be the lengths of the air column for the first and second resonances respectively.

$L_1 = 20.0 \text{ cm} = 0.20 \text{ m}$
$L_2 = 62.0 \text{ cm} = 0.62 \text{ m}$
$f = 400 \text{ Hz}$

The wavelength $\lambda$ is given by:
$\lambda = 2(L_2 - L_1)$

The speed of sound $v$ is:
$v = f\lambda = 2f(L_2 - L_1)$

Substituting the given values:
$v = 2 \times 400 \times (0.62 - 0.20)$
$v = 800 \times 0.42 = 336 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a resonance column experiment, a tuning fork of frequency $400 \text{ Hz}$ is utilized. The first resonance is noticed when the length of the air column is $20.0 \text{ cm}$, while the second resonance occurs when the air column length is $62.0 \text{ cm}$. How much distance above the open end does the pressure node form?
questions.solution:
Let $e$ be the end correction, which is the distance above the open end where the pressure node forms.

For the first resonance, the length of the air column is $L_1 = 20.0 \text{ cm}$. The relation is:

$L_1 + e = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}$

For the second resonance, the length of the air column is $L_2 = 62.0 \text{ cm}$. The relation is:

$L_2 + e = \dfrac{3\lambda}{4}$

Multiplying the first equation by $3$ and equating it to the second equation, we get:

$3(L_1 + e) = L_2 + e$

$3L_1 + 3e = L_2 + e$

$2e = L_2 - 3L_1$

$e = \dfrac{L_2 - 3L_1}{2}$

Substituting the given values:

$e = \dfrac{62.0 - 3(20.0)}{2}$

$e = \dfrac{62.0 - 60.0}{2}$

$e = \dfrac{2.0}{2} = 1.0 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe $P_2$ is identical to the first overtone frequency of a closed organ pipe $P_1$. If pipe $P_1$ has a length of $30 \text{ cm}$, what is the length of $P_2$?
questions.solution:
For a closed organ pipe $P_1$ of length $L_1$, the first overtone frequency is given by $f_1 = \dfrac{3v}{4L_1}$

For an open organ pipe $P_2$ of length $L_2$, the fundamental frequency is given by $f_2 = \dfrac{v}{2L_2}$

Given that $f_1 = f_2$

$\dfrac{3v}{4L_1} = \dfrac{v}{2L_2}$

$L_2 = \dfrac{2L_1}{3}$

Substituting $L_1 = 30 \text{ cm}$

$L_2 = \dfrac{2 \times 30}{3} = 20 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A copper rod of length $1.0 \text{ m}$ is clamped at its middle point. Determine the frequencies between $20 \text{ Hz}$ and $20{,}000 \text{ Hz}$ at which standing longitudinal waves can be established in the rod. The speed of sound in copper is $3.8 \text{ km s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The rod is clamped at its middle point, which means a node is formed at the center and antinodes are formed at the two free ends.

The distance from the clamped center to either free end is $\dfrac{L}{2}$. For standing waves, this distance must be an odd multiple of $\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$.

$\dfrac{L}{2} = (2n - 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{2L}{2n - 1}$

The corresponding frequencies are:

$f_n = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(2n - 1)v}{2L}$

Substituting $v = 3800 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $L = 1.0 \text{ m}$:

$f_n = \dfrac{(2n - 1) \times 3800}{2 \times 1.0} = 1900(2n - 1) \text{ Hz} = 1.9(2n - 1) \text{ kHz}$

The frequencies must lie between $20 \text{ Hz}$ and $20{,}000 \text{ Hz}$ ($20 \text{ kHz}$).

$1.9(2n - 1) \le 20$

$2n - 1 \le 10.52$

$2n \le 11.52 \Rightarrow n \le 5.76$

Since $n$ is an integer, $n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the greatest length of an organ pipe open at both ends such that its fundamental frequency lies within the normal hearing range ($20$–$20{,}000 \text{ Hz}$). The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of an organ pipe open at both ends is given by $f = \dfrac{v}{2L}$, where $v$ is the speed of sound and $L$ is the length of the pipe.

For the length $L$ to be maximum, the fundamental frequency $f$ must be minimum.

The minimum frequency in the normal hearing range is $f_{\text{min}} = 20 \text{ Hz}$.

Substituting the given values, we get $L_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{v}{2f_{\text{min}}}$.

$L_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{340}{2 \times 20} = \dfrac{340}{40} = 8.5 \text{ m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the fundamental frequency of vibration for an open organ pipe measuring $5 \text{ cm}$ in length. Assume the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
For an open organ pipe, the fundamental frequency is given by:

$f = \dfrac{v}{2L}$

Given $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $L = 5 \text{ cm} = 0.05 \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values:

$f = \dfrac{340}{2 \times 0.05}$

$f = \dfrac{340}{0.1}$

$f = 3400 \text{ Hz} = 3.4 \text{ kHz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An open organ pipe has a length of $5 \text{ cm}$. Identify the highest harmonic of this tube that falls within the audible range. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the audible frequency range is $20$–$20{,}000 \text{ Hz}$.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe is given by $f_1 = \dfrac{v}{2L}$

Substituting $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $L = 5 \text{ cm} = 0.05 \text{ m}$:

$f_1 = \dfrac{340}{2 \times 0.05} = \dfrac{340}{0.1} = 3400 \text{ Hz}$

The frequencies of the harmonics for an open pipe are given by $f_n = n f_1$, where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$

For the harmonic to fall within the audible range, its frequency must be less than or equal to $20{,}000 \text{ Hz}$:

$n \times 3400 \le 20{,}000$

$n \le \dfrac{20{,}000}{3400}$

$n \le 5.88$

Since $n$ must be an integer, the maximum possible value is $n = 5$.

Thus, the highest harmonic of this tube that falls within the audible range is $5$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electronically driven loudspeaker is positioned near the open end of a resonance column apparatus. The air column in the tube has a length of $80 \text{ cm}$. The loudspeaker's frequency can be adjusted between $20 \text{ Hz}$ and $2 \text{ kHz}$. Determine the frequencies at which the column will resonate. The speed of sound in air is $320 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
A resonance column apparatus acts as a pipe closed at one end (by the water surface) and open at the other.

The resonant frequencies for a closed pipe are given by:

$f = \dfrac{(2n + 1)v}{4L}$

where $v$ is the speed of sound, $L$ is the length of the air column, and $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$

Given $v = 320 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $L = 80 \text{ cm} = 0.8 \text{ m}$, we get:

$f = \dfrac{(2n + 1) \times 320}{4 \times 0.8} = 100(2n + 1) \text{ Hz}$

The loudspeaker's frequency range is $20 \text{ Hz}$ to $2000 \text{ Hz}$.

Therefore, $100(2n + 1) \le 2000$

$2n + 1 \le 20$

$n \le 9.5$

Since $n$ must be an integer, the possible values are $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9$.

The resonant frequencies are $100(2n + 1) \text{ Hz}$, where $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A piston is inserted into a cylindrical tube of small cross section whose other end is open. The tube resonates with a tuning fork having a frequency of $512 \text{ Hz}$. As the piston is gradually pulled out of the tube, a second resonance is observed when the piston has been displaced by a distance of $32.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the speed of sound in the air inside the tube.
questions.solution:
The distance between two consecutive resonant lengths in a closed organ pipe is equal to half the wavelength of the sound wave.

$\Delta L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$

Given that the displacement of the piston between the first and second resonance is $32.0 \text{ cm}$, we have:

$\Delta L = 32.0 \text{ cm} = 0.32 \text{ m}$

$\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 0.32 \Rightarrow \lambda = 0.64 \text{ m}$

The speed of sound $v$ is given by the relation:

$v = f \lambda$

Substituting the given frequency $f = 512 \text{ Hz}$ and the calculated wavelength $\lambda = 0.64 \text{ m}$:

$v = 512 \times 0.64 = 327.68 \text{ m/s}$

Rounding off to the nearest integer, we get $v \approx 328 \text{ m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A U-tube having unequal arm-lengths contains water. A tuning fork of frequency $440 \text{ Hz}$ can set up the air in the shorter arm in its fundamental mode of vibration, while the same tuning fork can set up the air in the longer arm in its first overtone vibration. Determine the lengths of the air columns. Disregard any end effect and assume that the speed of sound in air is $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The air columns in the U-tube act as closed organ pipes since they are closed by water at the bottom and open at the top.

The wavelength of the sound wave is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{330}{440} = 0.75 \text{ m} = 75 \text{ cm}$

For the shorter arm vibrating in its fundamental mode, the length of the air column $L_1$ is:

$L_1 = \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{75}{4} = 18.75 \text{ cm} \approx 18.8 \text{ cm}$

For the longer arm vibrating in its first overtone, the length of the air column $L_2$ is:

$L_2 = \dfrac{3\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{3 \times 75}{4} = 56.25 \text{ cm} \approx 56.3 \text{ cm}$

The lengths of the air columns are $18.8 \text{ cm}$ and $56.3 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the arrangement depicted in the figure, a wire with a mass of $4.00 \text{ g}$ oscillates in its second harmonic. This sets the air column in the tube into vibrations in its fundamental mode. Provided that the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the tension in the wire.
questions.solution:
For the air column in the tube, it is closed at one end (water surface) and open at the other. It vibrates in its fundamental mode.
The fundamental frequency of the closed organ pipe is given by:
$f_a = \dfrac{v_s}{4L_a}$
where $v_s = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ is the speed of sound and $L_a = 1.0 \text{ m}$ is the length of the air column.
$f_a = \dfrac{340}{4 \times 1.0} = 85 \text{ Hz}$

The wire oscillates in its second harmonic and sets the air column into resonance, so the frequency of the wire is equal to the frequency of the air column.
$f_w = f_a = 85 \text{ Hz}$

The frequency of the $n$-th harmonic of a stretched string is:
$f_w = \dfrac{n}{2L_w} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$
For the second harmonic, $n = 2$. The length of the wire is $L_w = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$.
The linear mass density $\mu$ of the wire is:
$\mu = \dfrac{m}{L_w} = \dfrac{4.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}}{0.4 \text{ m}} = 10^{-2} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$

Substituting the values into the frequency formula:
$85 = \dfrac{2}{2 \times 0.4} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{10^{-2}}}$
$85 = \dfrac{1}{0.4} \sqrt{100 T}$
$85 = 2.5 \times 10 \sqrt{T}$
$85 = 25 \sqrt{T}$
$\sqrt{T} = \dfrac{85}{25} = 3.4$

Squaring both sides to find the tension $T$:
$T = (3.4)^2 = 11.56 \text{ N}$

Rounding to one decimal place, we get $T \approx 11.6 \text{ N}$.
questions.question: In the arrangement depicted in the figure, a wire with a mass of $4.00 \text{ g}$ oscillates in its second harmonic. This sets the air column in the tube into vibrations in its fundamental mode. Provided that the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the tension in the wire.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an open organ pipe, two successive resonance frequencies are $1620 \text{ Hz}$ and $2268 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the length of the tube. The speed of sound in air is $324 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The difference between two successive resonance frequencies is:

$\Delta f = 2268 - 1620 = 648 \text{ Hz}$

For an organ pipe, the difference between successive resonance frequencies is $\dfrac{v}{2L}$.

$\dfrac{v}{2L} = 648$

$\dfrac{324}{2L} = 648$

$2L = \dfrac{324}{648} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$L = \dfrac{1}{4} \text{ m} = 25 \text{ cm}$
