When the room temperature experiences a small variation from $T$ to $T + \Delta T$, the fundamental frequency of an organ pipe shifts from $
u$ to $
u + \Delta
u$. Which of the following expressions correctly relates the fractional change in frequency to the fractional change in temperature?
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of an organ pipe is given by $ u = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$, where $v$ is the speed of sound and $\lambda$ is the wavelength.

The speed of sound in a gas at absolute temperature $T$ is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma R T}{M}}$.

Thus, the fundamental frequency is directly proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature:

$ u \propto \sqrt{T}$

$ u = k T^{1/2}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides:

$\ln u = \ln k + \dfrac{1}{2} \ln T$

Differentiating both sides for small variations:

$\dfrac{\Delta u}{ u} = \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{\Delta T}{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length $30.0 \text{ cm}$ and mass $10.0 \text{ g}$ is secured at both ends and vibrates in its fundamental mode. A closed organ pipe measuring $50.0 \text{ cm}$ in length is positioned with its open end close to the wire, and it is driven into resonance in its fundamental mode by the vibrating wire. Determine the tension in the wire. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of the closed organ pipe is given by:

$f = \dfrac{v}{4L_c}$

Substituting $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $L_c = 0.5 \text{ m}$:

$f = \dfrac{340}{4 \times 0.5} = 170 \text{ Hz}$

Since the wire is in resonance with the pipe, its fundamental frequency is also $170 \text{ Hz}$. The fundamental frequency of a stretched wire is given by:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2L_w} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

Here, the length of the wire is $L_w = 0.3 \text{ m}$ and its linear mass density is $\mu = \dfrac{m}{L_w} = \dfrac{10 \times 10^{-3}}{0.3} = \dfrac{1}{30} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$.

Substituting the known values into the frequency formula:

$170 = \dfrac{1}{2 \times 0.3} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{1/30}}$

$170 \times 0.6 = \sqrt{30T}$

$102 = \sqrt{30T}$

Squaring both sides:

$10404 = 30T$

$T = \dfrac{10404}{30} = 346.8 \text{ N}$

Rounding off, the tension in the wire is approximately $347 \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An unknown tuning fork produces $5$ beats per second with a second tuning fork that causes a closed organ pipe of length $40 \text{ cm}$ to vibrate in its fundamental mode. When the first tuning fork is loaded slightly with wax, the beat frequency decreases. Determine the original frequency of the first tuning fork. Assume the speed of sound in air is $320 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a closed organ pipe is given by $n_2 = \dfrac{v}{4L}$.

Substituting the given values, $n_2 = \dfrac{320}{4 \times 0.4} = 200 \text{ Hz}$.

Since the unknown tuning fork produces $5$ beats per second with the second tuning fork, its frequency is $n_1 = n_2 \pm 5 = 200 \pm 5$.

Thus, $n_1$ is either $205 \text{ Hz}$ or $195 \text{ Hz}$.

When a tuning fork is loaded with wax, its frequency decreases.

If $n_1 = 205 \text{ Hz}$, a decrease in frequency will bring it closer to $200 \text{ Hz}$, resulting in a beat frequency less than $5 \text{ Hz}$. This matches the given condition.

If $n_1 = 195 \text{ Hz}$, a decrease in frequency will take it further away from $200 \text{ Hz}$, resulting in a beat frequency greater than $5 \text{ Hz}$. This contradicts the given condition.

Therefore, the original frequency of the first tuning fork is $205 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A piano wire $A$ vibrates with a fundamental frequency of $600 \text{ Hz}$. A second identical wire $B$ generates $6$ beats per second with it when the tension in $A$ is slightly increased. Determine the ratio of the tension in $A$ to the tension in $B$.
questions.solution:
The initial fundamental frequency of wire A and the identical wire B is $f_B = 600 \text{ Hz}$.

When the tension in wire A is slightly increased, its frequency increases. Since it produces $6$ beats per second with wire B, the new frequency of wire A is:

$f_A = 600 + 6 = 606 \text{ Hz}$

The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is given by $f = \dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$, which implies $f \propto \sqrt{T}$.

Therefore, the ratio of the tension in A to the tension in B is:

$\dfrac{T_A}{T_B} = \left(\dfrac{f_A}{f_B}\right)^2$

$\dfrac{T_A}{T_B} = \left(\dfrac{606}{600}\right)^2 = (1.01)^2 = 1.0201 \approx 1.02$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tuning fork with a frequency of $256 \text{ Hz}$ generates $4$ beats per second alongside a wire of length $25 \text{ cm}$ vibrating in its fundamental mode. Upon slightly shortening the length of the wire, the beat frequency decreases. Determine the minimum length by which the wire must be shortened to produce zero beats with the tuning fork.
questions.solution:
Frequency of the tuning fork is $f_t = 256 \text{ Hz}$.

Since $4$ beats per second are heard, the possible frequencies of the wire are $f_w = 256 \pm 4$, which gives $260 \text{ Hz}$ or $252 \text{ Hz}$.

The fundamental frequency of a stretched wire is given by $f_w = \dfrac{v}{2L}$. As the length $L$ of the wire is shortened, its frequency $f_w$ increases.

It is given that upon shortening the wire, the beat frequency decreases. This is only possible if the initial frequency of the wire was lower than the tuning fork's frequency. Thus, the initial frequency of the wire is $f_{w1} = 252 \text{ Hz}$.

To produce zero beats, the new frequency of the wire must be equal to the frequency of the tuning fork, so $f_{w2} = 256 \text{ Hz}$.

Since the frequency is inversely proportional to the length ($f \propto \dfrac{1}{L}$), we have:

$f_{w1} L_1 = f_{w2} L_2$

$252 \times 25 = 256 \times L_2$

$L_2 = \dfrac{252 \times 25}{256} \approx 24.61 \text{ cm}$

The length by which the wire must be shortened is:

$\Delta L = L_1 - L_2 = 25 - 24.61 = 0.39 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A traffic policeman stationed on a road blows a whistle that emits a main frequency of $2.00 \text{ kHz}$. Determine the apparent frequency heard by a scooter-driver who is approaching the policeman at a speed of $36.0 \text{ km/h}$. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
The frequency of the source is $f = 2.00 \text{ kHz}$.

The speed of the observer is $v_o = 36.0 \text{ km/h} = 36.0 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 10.0 \text{ m/s}$.

The speed of sound is $v = 340 \text{ m/s}$ and the speed of the source is $v_s = 0$.

Using the Doppler effect formula for an observer approaching a stationary source:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_o}{v} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f' = 2.00 \times \left( \dfrac{340 + 10}{340} \right)$

$f' = 2.00 \times \left( \dfrac{350}{340} \right)$

$f' = 2.00 \times \dfrac{35}{34} \approx 2.058 \text{ kHz}$

Rounding to two decimal places, $f' \approx 2.06 \text{ kHz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car's horn emits sound having a dominant frequency of $2400 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the apparent dominant frequency heard by a person standing on the road ahead of the car, given that the car approaches at $18.0 \text{ km/h}$. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
The speed of the car (source) is $v_s = 18.0 \text{ km/h} = 18.0 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 5 \text{ m/s}$.

The observer is stationary, so $v_o = 0$.

Using the Doppler effect formula for a source approaching a stationary observer:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f' = 2400 \left( \dfrac{340}{340 - 5} \right)$

$f' = 2400 \left( \dfrac{340}{335} \right)$

$f' \approx 2435.8 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the apparent frequency is $2436 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person travelling in a car moving at $72 \text{ km/h}$ blows a whistle that emits a wave of frequency $1250 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the frequency heard by another person standing on the road in front of the car. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
Speed of the car (source), $v_s = 72 \text{ km/h} = 72 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 20 \text{ m/s}$

Speed of sound, $v = 340 \text{ m/s}$

Actual frequency of the whistle, $f_0 = 1250 \text{ Hz}$

Since the car is moving towards the stationary observer, the apparent frequency $f$ is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f = 1250 \left( \dfrac{340}{340 - 20} \right)$

$f = 1250 \left( \dfrac{340}{320} \right)$

$f = 1250 \times \dfrac{17}{16}$

$f = 1328.125 \text{ Hz}$

The frequency heard by the person is approximately $1328 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person travelling in a car moving at $72 \text{ km/h}$ blows a whistle that emits a wave of frequency $1250 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the frequency heard by another person standing on the road behind the car. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
Speed of the car, $v_s = 72 \text{ km/h} = 72 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 20 \text{ m/s}$

Speed of sound, $v = 340 \text{ m/s}$

Actual frequency, $f = 1250 \text{ Hz}$

Since the car is moving away from the stationary observer, the apparent frequency $f'$ is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_s} \right)$

$f' = 1250 \left( \dfrac{340}{340 + 20} \right)$

$f' = 1250 \left( \dfrac{340}{360} \right)$

$f' = 1250 \times \dfrac{17}{18}$

$f' \approx 1180.55 \text{ Hz} \approx 1181 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Approaching a platform at a speed of $54 \text{ km/h}$, a train sounds a whistle. An observer on the platform measures its frequency to be $1620 \text{ Hz}$. The train passes the platform without slowing down while keeping the whistle on. What frequency will the observer hear after the train has crossed the platform? The speed of sound in air is $332 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
Speed of the train, $v_s = 54 \text{ km/h} = 54 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 15 \text{ m/s}$

Apparent frequency during approach, $f_1 = 1620 \text{ Hz}$

Speed of sound, $v = 332 \text{ m/s}$

By Doppler's effect, the apparent frequency when the train approaches the stationary observer is given by:

$f_1 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right)$

$1620 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{332}{332 - 15} \right) = f_0 \left( \dfrac{332}{317} \right)$

$f_0 = 1620 \times \dfrac{317}{332}$

When the train crosses the platform and moves away, the apparent frequency heard by the observer is:

$f_2 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_s} \right)$

Substituting the value of $f_0$:

$f_2 = 1620 \times \left( \dfrac{317}{332} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{332}{332 + 15} \right)$

$f_2 = 1620 \times \dfrac{317}{347}$

$f_2 \approx 1480 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bat flies at a speed of $6 \text{ m/s}$ between two parallel walls while emitting an ultrasonic wave of frequency $4.5 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the two frequencies heard by the bat, as well as the beat frequency between them. The speed of sound is $330 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
The bat acts as both a moving source and a moving observer.

For the wall the bat is approaching, the frequency of the reflected wave heard by the bat is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f_1 = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_b}{v - v_b} \right)$

Substituting $v = 330 \text{ m/s}$, $v_b = 6 \text{ m/s}$, and $f = 4.5 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$:

$f_1 = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{330 + 6}{330 - 6} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{336}{324} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{28}{27} \right) \approx 4.67 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$

For the wall the bat is moving away from, the frequency of the reflected wave heard by the bat is:

$f_2 = f \left( \dfrac{v - v_b}{v + v_b} \right)$

$f_2 = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{330 - 6}{330 + 6} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{324}{336} \right) = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{27}{28} \right) \approx 4.34 \times 10^4 \text{ Hz}$

The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies heard by the bat:

$f_{\text{beat}} = f_1 - f_2 = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{28}{27} - \dfrac{27}{28} \right)$

$f_{\text{beat}} = 4.5 \times 10^4 \left( \dfrac{784 - 729}{756} \right) = 45000 \times \dfrac{55}{756} \approx 3274 \text{ Hz} \approx 3270 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bullet travels past a person at a speed of $220 \text{ m/s}$. Determine the fractional change in the frequency of the whistling sound perceived by the person as the bullet crosses them. Take the speed of sound in air to be $330 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
Let the actual frequency of the whistling sound be $f_0$.

When the bullet approaches the stationary person, the apparent frequency $f_1$ is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f_1 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right)$

Substituting $v = 330 \text{ m/s}$ and $v_s = 220 \text{ m/s}$:

$f_1 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{330}{330 - 220} \right) = f_0 \left( \dfrac{330}{110} \right) = 3f_0$

When the bullet recedes from the person, the apparent frequency $f_2$ is:

$f_2 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_s} \right)$

$f_2 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{330}{330 + 220} \right) = f_0 \left( \dfrac{330}{550} \right) = 0.6f_0$

The change in the perceived frequency as the bullet crosses the person is:

$\Delta f = f_1 - f_2 = 3f_0 - 0.6f_0 = 2.4f_0$

The fractional change in the frequency is:

$\dfrac{\Delta f}{f_0} = \dfrac{2.4f_0}{f_0} = 2.4$

Answer: $2.4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two electric trains travel in the same direction along the same track at a uniform speed of $72 \text{ km/h}$, maintaining a separation of $2.4 \text{ km}$. Both trains sound brief whistles simultaneously. At the instant the whistling occurs, a person is located at a perpendicular distance of $500 \text{ m}$ from the track and is equidistant from the two trains. Given that the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$ and the original frequency of both whistles is $500 \text{ Hz}$, determine the frequencies heard by the person.
questions.solution:
Speed of the trains, $v_s = 72 \text{ km/h} = 72 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 20 \text{ m/s}$.

The separation between the two trains is $2.4 \text{ km} = 2400 \text{ m}$. Since the person is equidistant from both trains at the instant of whistling, the distance along the track from the person's projection to each train is $\dfrac{2400}{2} = 1200 \text{ m}$.

The perpendicular distance of the person from the track is $500 \text{ m}$.

The straight-line distance from each train to the person is:
$d = \sqrt{1200^2 + 500^2} = 1300 \text{ m}$

Let $\theta$ be the angle between the track and the line joining the train to the person. Then:
$\cos \theta = \dfrac{1200}{1300} = \dfrac{12}{13}$

One train is approaching the person, and the other is moving away. The component of the velocity of the trains along the line of sight to the person is:
$v_{s \parallel} = v_s \cos \theta = 20 \times \dfrac{12}{13} = \dfrac{240}{13} \text{ m/s}$

Using the Doppler effect formula, the apparent frequency of the approaching train is:
$f_1 = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_{s \parallel}} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{340}{340 - \dfrac{240}{13}} \right)$

$f_1 = 500 \left( \dfrac{340 \times 13}{340 \times 13 - 240} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{4420}{4180} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{221}{209} \right) \approx 528.7 \text{ Hz} \approx 529 \text{ Hz}$

The apparent frequency of the receding train is:
$f_2 = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_{s \parallel}} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{340}{340 + \dfrac{240}{13}} \right)$

$f_2 = 500 \left( \dfrac{340 \times 13}{340 \times 13 + 240} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{4420}{4660} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{221}{233} \right) \approx 474.2 \text{ Hz} \approx 474 \text{ Hz}$

Thus, the frequencies heard by the person are $529 \text{ Hz}$ and $474 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A violin player travelling on a slow train sounds a $440 \text{ Hz}$ note, while another violin player standing beside the track produces the identical note. As the train approaches the person on the ground when they are near each other, the person on the ground detects $4.0$ beats per second. Given the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$, determine the speed of the train.
questions.solution:
Let $f_0$ be the actual frequency of the violin, $v$ be the speed of sound, and $v_s$ be the speed of the train.

Given $f_0 = 440 \text{ Hz}$ and $v = 340 \text{ m/s}$.

The apparent frequency $f'$ heard by the stationary person on the ground from the approaching train is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f' = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right)$

The person hears a beat frequency of $4.0 \text{ Hz}$ between the stationary violin and the approaching violin. Thus, the apparent frequency is:

$f' = f_0 + f_b = 440 + 4 = 444 \text{ Hz}$

Substituting the values into the Doppler effect formula:

$444 = 440 \left( \dfrac{340}{340 - v_s} \right)$

$444(340 - v_s) = 440 \times 340$

$150960 - 444 v_s = 149600$

$444 v_s = 1360$

$v_s = \dfrac{1360}{444} = \dfrac{340}{111} \text{ m/s}$

To convert the speed from $\text{m/s}$ to $\text{km/h}$, we multiply by $\dfrac{18}{5}$:

$v_s = \dfrac{340}{111} \times \dfrac{18}{5} \text{ km/h} = \dfrac{1224}{111} \text{ km/h} \approx 11.03 \text{ km/h}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the speed of the train is $11 \text{ km/h}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A violin player travelling on a slow train sounds a $440 \text{ Hz}$ note, while another violin player standing beside the track produces the identical note. As the train approaches the person on the ground when they are near each other, the person on the ground detects $4.0$ beats per second. Given the speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$, what beat frequency is detected by the player on the train?
questions.solution:
Let $f = 440 \text{ Hz}$ be the actual frequency of the note.

Let $v$ be the speed of sound and $v_s$ be the speed of the train.

For the observer on the ground, the source (train) is moving towards them. The apparent frequency heard by the person on the ground is:

$f_1 = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right)$

The beat frequency detected by the ground observer is:

$\Delta f_1 = f_1 - f = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} - 1 \right) = f \left( \dfrac{v_s}{v - v_s} \right) = 4.0 \text{ Hz}$

For the observer on the train, the source on the ground is stationary and the observer is moving towards it. The apparent frequency heard by the player on the train is:

$f_2 = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_s}{v} \right)$

The beat frequency detected by the train observer is:

$\Delta f_2 = f_2 - f = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_s}{v} - 1 \right) = f \left( \dfrac{v_s}{v} \right)$

Comparing $\Delta f_1$ and $\Delta f_2$:

$\Delta f_2 = f \left( \dfrac{v_s}{v - v_s} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{v - v_s}{v} \right) = \Delta f_1 \left( \dfrac{v - v_s}{v} \right)$

$\Delta f_2 = 4.0 \left( 1 - \dfrac{v_s}{v} \right)$

Since the train is moving, $v_s > 0$, which implies $\left( 1 - \dfrac{v_s}{v} \right) < 1$.

Therefore, $\Delta f_2 < 4.0 \text{ Hz}$.

The beat frequency detected by the player on the train is a little less than $4.0 \text{ beats/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical tuning forks vibrating at a common frequency of $256\text{ Hz}$ are held stationary at some distance apart. A listener runs between the tuning forks at a speed of $3.0 \text{ m/s}$, approaching one tuning fork while receding from the other, as shown in the figure. Determine the beat frequency observed by the listener. Assume the speed of sound in air to be $332 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
The apparent frequency heard by the listener from the tuning fork being approached is given by Doppler's effect:

$f_1 = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_L}{v} \right)$

The apparent frequency heard from the tuning fork being receded from is:

$f_2 = f \left( \dfrac{v - v_L}{v} \right)$

The beat frequency observed by the listener is the difference between these two frequencies:

$f_b = f_1 - f_2 = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_L}{v} \right) - f \left( \dfrac{v - v_L}{v} \right)$

$f_b = f \left( \dfrac{2v_L}{v} \right)$

Substituting the given values ($f = 256 \text{ Hz}$, $v_L = 3.0 \text{ m/s}$, $v = 332 \text{ m/s}$):

$f_b = 256 \times \left( \dfrac{2 \times 3.0}{332} \right)$

$f_b = \dfrac{1536}{332} \approx 4.6 \text{ Hz}$

A listener runs between the tuning forks at a speed of $3.0 \text{ m/s}$, approaching one tuning fork while receding from the other, as shown in the figure. Determine the beat frequency observed by the listener. Assume the speed of sound in air to be $332 \text{ m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As shown in the figure, a person is standing somewhere between two identical tuning forks that are each vibrating at $512 \text{ Hz}$. If both tuning forks travel towards the right at a speed of $5.5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the number of beats heard by the listener. The speed of sound in air is $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Given:
Frequency of tuning forks, $f = 512 \text{ Hz}$
Speed of tuning forks, $v_s = 5.5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$
Speed of sound, $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The tuning fork on the left moves towards the stationary listener. The apparent frequency heard by the listener is:
$f_1 = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right)$

The tuning fork on the right moves away from the stationary listener. The apparent frequency heard by the listener is:
$f_2 = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_s} \right)$

The number of beats heard by the listener is the difference between these two apparent frequencies:
$f_B = f_1 - f_2 = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} - \dfrac{v}{v + v_s} \right)$

$f_B = fv \left( \dfrac{v + v_s - (v - v_s)}{v^2 - v_s^2} \right) = \dfrac{2 f v v_s}{v^2 - v_s^2}$

Since $v_s \ll v$, we can approximate $v^2 - v_s^2 \approx v^2$:
$f_B \approx \dfrac{2 f v v_s}{v^2} = \dfrac{2 f v_s}{v}$

Substituting the given values:
$f_B = \dfrac{2 \times 512 \times 5.5}{330}$

$f_B = \dfrac{512 \times 11}{330} = \dfrac{512}{30} \approx 17.067 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding to one decimal place, we get $17.1 \text{ Hz}$.

If both tuning forks travel towards the right at a speed of $5.5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the number of beats heard by the listener. The speed of sound in air is $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small source of sound vibrating at a frequency of $500 \text{ Hz}$ is rotated in a circle of radius $100/\pi \text{ cm}$ with a constant angular speed of $5.0$ revolutions per second. A listener is situated in the plane of the circle. Determine the minimum and maximum frequencies of the sound observed. The speed of sound in air is $332 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The linear speed of the source is given by $v_s = R\omega$.

Given the radius $R = \dfrac{100}{\pi} \text{ cm} = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \text{ m}$ and angular speed $\omega = 5.0 \text{ rev/s} = 10\pi \text{ rad/s}$, we get:

$v_s = \left(\dfrac{1}{\pi}\right)(10\pi) = 10 \text{ m/s}$

The maximum frequency is observed when the source moves directly towards the listener:

$f_{max} = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{332}{332 - 10} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{332}{322} \right) \approx 515.5 \text{ Hz}$

The minimum frequency is observed when the source moves directly away from the listener:

$f_{min} = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_s} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{332}{332 + 10} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{332}{342} \right) \approx 485.4 \text{ Hz}$

The closest values are $485 \text{ Hz}$ and $515 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two trains are moving towards each other, each with a speed of $90 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. If one train sounds a whistle at $500 \text{ Hz}$, determine the apparent frequency heard in the other train. The speed of sound in air is $350 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Speed of each train, $v_s = v_o = 90 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 90 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 25 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Speed of sound, $v = 350 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Actual frequency, $f = 500 \text{ Hz}$

Using the formula for Doppler effect when both source and observer are moving towards each other:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_o}{v - v_s} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f' = 500 \left( \dfrac{350 + 25}{350 - 25} \right)$

$f' = 500 \left( \dfrac{375}{325} \right)$

$f' = 500 \left( \dfrac{15}{13} \right)$

$f' = \dfrac{7500}{13} \approx 576.92 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding off to the nearest integer, the apparent frequency is $577 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A traffic policeman blows a whistle to halt an approaching car-driver. The car-driver fails to stop and later argues in court that, due to the Doppler shift, the frequency of the whistle reaching him could have exceeded the audible limit of $20 \text{ kHz}$, making it impossible to hear. Tests revealed that the whistle produces sound at a frequency close to $16 \text{ kHz}$. Assuming the driver's argument is correct, what was the speed of the car? (Take the speed of sound in air to be $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.)
questions.solution:
The frequency heard by the approaching driver is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_c}{v} \right)$

where $f'$ is the apparent frequency, $f$ is the actual frequency, $v$ is the speed of sound, and $v_c$ is the speed of the car.

Given $f' = 20 \text{ kHz}$, $f = 16 \text{ kHz}$, and $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, substituting these values:

$20 = 16 \left( \dfrac{330 + v_c}{330} \right)$

$\dfrac{5}{4} = 1 + \dfrac{v_c}{330}$

$\dfrac{v_c}{330} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$v_c = \dfrac{330}{4} = 82.5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Converting the speed from $\text{m s}^{-1}$ to $\text{km h}^{-1}$:

$v_c = 82.5 \times \dfrac{18}{5} \text{ km h}^{-1} = 297 \text{ km h}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car travelling at $108 \text{ km h}^{-1}$ encounters another car ahead of it moving in the same direction at $72 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. The first car sounds a horn with a dominant frequency of $800 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the apparent frequency heard by the driver in the front car. The speed of sound in air is $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Speed of the first car (source), $v_s = 108 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 108 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 30 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Speed of the second car (observer), $v_o = 72 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 72 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Actual frequency of the horn, $f = 800 \text{ Hz}$

Speed of sound, $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The source is moving towards the observer and the observer is moving away from the source.

Using the Doppler effect formula for apparent frequency:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v - v_o}{v - v_s} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f' = 800 \left( \dfrac{330 - 20}{330 - 30} \right)$

$f' = 800 \left( \dfrac{310}{300} \right)$

$f' = 800 \times \dfrac{31}{30}$

$f' = \dfrac{2480}{3} \approx 826.67 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding off to the nearest integer, the apparent frequency is $827 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a calm sea, two submarines approach one another. Relative to the water, the first submarine moves at $36 \text{ km h}^{-1}$ while the second submarine moves at $54 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. The first submarine emits a sound signal (sonar) with a frequency of $2000 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the frequency at which the second submarine receives this signal. Assume the speed of sound waves in water is $1500 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Speed of the first submarine (source), $v_s = 36 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 36 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Speed of the second submarine (observer), $v_o = 54 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 54 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Speed of sound in water, $v = 1500 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Actual frequency of the signal, $f = 2000 \text{ Hz}$

Using the Doppler effect formula for an approaching source and observer:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_o}{v - v_s} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f' = 2000 \left( \dfrac{1500 + 15}{1500 - 10} \right)$

$f' = 2000 \left( \dfrac{1515}{1490} \right)$

$f' = \dfrac{303000}{149} \approx 2033.56 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding to the nearest integer gives $2034 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a calm sea, two submarines approach one another. Relative to the water, the first submarine moves at $36 \text{ km h}^{-1}$ while the second submarine moves at $54 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. The first submarine emits a sound signal (sonar) with a frequency of $2000 \text{ Hz}$, which is then reflected by the second submarine. Determine the frequency of the reflected signal as received by the first submarine. Assume the speed of sound waves in water is $1500 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Speed of the first submarine, $v_1 = 36 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Speed of the second submarine, $v_2 = 54 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Speed of sound in water, $v = 1500 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Frequency of the emitted signal, $f_0 = 2000 \text{ Hz}$

The frequency received by the second submarine is given by the Doppler effect formula for an observer moving towards a source and a source moving towards the observer:

$f_1 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v + v_2}{v - v_1} \right)$

The second submarine reflects this signal, acting as a moving source, while the first submarine acts as a moving observer. The frequency of the reflected signal received by the first submarine is:

$f_2 = f_1 \left( \dfrac{v + v_1}{v - v_2} \right)$

Substituting $f_1$ into the equation for $f_2$:

$f_2 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v + v_2}{v - v_1} \right) \left( \dfrac{v + v_1}{v - v_2} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f_2 = 2000 \left( \dfrac{1500 + 15}{1500 - 10} \right) \left( \dfrac{1500 + 10}{1500 - 15} \right)$

$f_2 = 2000 \left( \dfrac{1515}{1490} \right) \left( \dfrac{1510}{1485} \right)$

$f_2 = 2000 \left( \dfrac{303}{298} \right) \left( \dfrac{302}{297} \right)$

$f_2 = 2000 \left( \dfrac{101}{99} \right) \left( \dfrac{151}{149} \right)$

$f_2 = 2000 \left( \dfrac{15251}{14751} \right)$

$f_2 \approx 2067.79 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the frequency is $2068 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small source of sound executes simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of $17 \text{ cm}$. A detector is positioned along the source's line of motion. The source emits a sound of frequency $800 \text{ Hz}$ that travels at a speed of $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Determine the time period of the source if the width of the frequency band observed by the detector is $8 \text{ Hz}$.
questions.solution:
The maximum velocity of the source executing simple harmonic motion is $v_{max} = A\omega = A\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)$.

The maximum frequency observed by the detector occurs when the source moves towards it with maximum velocity:

$f_{max} = f_0 \left(\dfrac{v}{v - v_{max}}\right)$

The minimum frequency observed occurs when the source moves away from it with maximum velocity:

$f_{min} = f_0 \left(\dfrac{v}{v + v_{max}}\right)$

The width of the frequency band is given by $\Delta f = f_{max} - f_{min}$:

$\Delta f = f_0 v \left( \dfrac{1}{v - v_{max}} - \dfrac{1}{v + v_{max}} \right) = f_0 v \left( \dfrac{2v_{max}}{v^2 - v_{max}^2} \right)$

Since $v_{max}$ is much smaller than $v$, we can approximate $v^2 - v_{max}^2 \approx v^2$, which gives:

$\Delta f \approx f_0 \left( \dfrac{2v_{max}}{v} \right)$

Substituting the given values $\Delta f = 8 \text{ Hz}$, $f_0 = 800 \text{ Hz}$, and $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$8 = 800 \left( \dfrac{2v_{max}}{340} \right)$

$1 = 100 \left( \dfrac{2v_{max}}{340} \right) \Rightarrow v_{max} = \dfrac{340}{200} = 1.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Now, using the relation for maximum velocity in SHM with $A = 17 \text{ cm} = 0.17 \text{ m}$:

$v_{max} = A \left( \dfrac{2\pi}{T} \right)$

$1.7 = 0.17 \times \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$

$10 = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} \Rightarrow T = \dfrac{\pi}{5} \text{ s}$

$T \approx 0.628 \text{ s} \approx 0.63 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A boy riding on his bike is travelling towards the east at a speed of $4\sqrt{2} \text{ m s}^{-1}$. At a particular instant, he generates a sound pulse with a frequency of $1650 \text{ Hz}$ which travels through the air at a speed of $334 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Another boy is standing on the ground $45^\circ$ south of east relative to him. Determine the frequency of the pulse as received by the second boy.
questions.solution:
The velocity of the source is $v_s = 4\sqrt{2} \text{ m s}^{-1}$ towards the east.

The observer is stationary, so $v_o = 0$. The position of the observer relative to the source is $45^\circ$ south of east.

The component of the source's velocity along the line joining the source and the observer is:

$v_{s,\text{eff}} = v_s \cos(45^\circ) = 4\sqrt{2} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 4 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Using the Doppler effect formula for a stationary observer and a moving source, the apparent frequency $f'$ is given by:

$f' = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_{s,\text{eff}}} \right)$

Substituting the given values $f_0 = 1650 \text{ Hz}$ and $v = 334 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$f' = 1650 \left( \dfrac{334}{334 - 4} \right)$

$f' = 1650 \left( \dfrac{334}{330} \right)$

$f' = 5 \times 334 = 1670 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sound source is fixed at the origin and continuously emits sound at a frequency of $660 \text{ Hz}$. The sound propagates through air at a speed of $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. A listener travels along the line $x = 336 \text{ m}$ with a constant speed of $26 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the frequency of the sound observed by the listener when he is positioned at $y = -140 \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
The position of the source is $S(0, 0)$ and the listener is at $L(336, -140)$.

The distance between the source and the listener is $d = \sqrt{336^2 + (-140)^2} = \sqrt{112896 + 19600} = 364 \text{ m}$.

Assuming the listener moves in the positive $y$-direction, the velocity of the listener is $\vec{v}_L = 26 \hat{j} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The unit vector from the listener to the source is $\hat{u} = \dfrac{-336 \hat{i} + 140 \hat{j}}{364} = -\dfrac{12}{13} \hat{i} + \dfrac{5}{13} \hat{j}$.

The component of the listener's velocity towards the source is $v_{L \parallel} = \vec{v}_L \cdot \hat{u} = (26 \hat{j}) \cdot \left( -\dfrac{12}{13} \hat{i} + \dfrac{5}{13} \hat{j} \right) = 26 \times \dfrac{5}{13} = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Using the Doppler effect formula, the observed frequency is:

$f' = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v + v_{L \parallel}}{v} \right)$

$f' = 660 \left( \dfrac{330 + 10}{330} \right) = 660 \times \dfrac{340}{330} = 680 \text{ Hz}$.

Answer: $680 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sound source is fixed at the origin and continuously emits sound at a frequency of $660 \text{ Hz}$. The sound propagates through air at a speed of $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. A listener travels along the line $x = 336 \text{ m}$ with a constant speed of $26 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the frequency of the sound observed by the listener when he is positioned at $y = 140 \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
The position of the sound source is at the origin $(0, 0)$.

The position of the listener is $(336, 140)$.

The distance between the source and the listener is:

$r = \sqrt{336^2 + 140^2} = \sqrt{112896 + 19600} = \sqrt{132496} = 364 \text{ m}$

Assuming the listener travels in the positive y-direction, the velocity of the listener is $\vec{v}_L = 26 \hat{j} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The unit vector along the line joining the source to the listener is:

$\hat{r} = \dfrac{336 \hat{i} + 140 \hat{j}}{364} = \dfrac{12}{13} \hat{i} + \dfrac{5}{13} \hat{j}$

The component of the listener's velocity along the line of sight (away from the source) is:

$v_o = \vec{v}_L \cdot \hat{r} = (26 \hat{j}) \cdot \left( \dfrac{12}{13} \hat{i} + \dfrac{5}{13} \hat{j} \right) = 26 \times \dfrac{5}{13} = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Since the listener is moving away from the source, the apparent frequency $f'$ is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f' = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v - v_o}{v} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f' = 660 \left( \dfrac{330 - 10}{330} \right) = 660 \left( \dfrac{320}{330} \right) = 2 \times 320 = 640 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A train travelling at $108 \text{ km h}^{-1}$ towards east whistles with a dominant frequency of $500 \text{ Hz}$. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$. What frequency will a passenger sitting near the open window hear?
questions.solution:
The passenger and the whistle are on the same train.

The relative velocity between the source of sound (whistle) and the observer (passenger) is zero.

According to the Doppler effect, the apparent frequency is given by $f' = f \left( \dfrac{v - v_o}{v - v_s} \right)$.

Since both the source and the observer are moving with the same velocity in the same direction, $v_o = v_s$.

Substituting these values, we get $f' = f = 500 \text{ Hz}$.

The frequency heard by the passenger remains unchanged at $500 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A train travelling at $108 \text{ km h}^{-1}$ towards east whistles with a dominant frequency of $500 \text{ Hz}$. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$. What frequency will a person standing near the track hear whom the train has just passed?
questions.solution:
Speed of the train, $v_s = 108 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 108 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 30 \text{ m/s}$

Speed of sound, $v = 340 \text{ m/s}$

Actual frequency, $f_0 = 500 \text{ Hz}$

Since the train has just passed the person, it is moving away from the stationary observer.

Using the Doppler effect formula for a source moving away from a stationary observer:

$f = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_s} \right)$

Substituting the values:

$f = 500 \left( \dfrac{340}{340 + 30} \right)$

$f = 500 \left( \dfrac{340}{370} \right)$

$f = \dfrac{17000}{37} \approx 459.46 \text{ Hz}$

The frequency heard by the person is approximately $459 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A train travelling at $108 \text{ km h}^{-1}$ towards east whistles with a dominant frequency of $500 \text{ Hz}$. The speed of sound in air is $340 \text{ m/s}$. A wind begins blowing towards east at a speed of $36 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. Determine the frequencies heard by a passenger in the train and by a person standing near the track whom the train has just passed.
options: $500 \text{ Hz}$ by the passenger and $459 \text{ Hz}$ by the person near the track
$500 \text{ Hz}$ by the passenger and $472 \text{ Hz}$ by the person near the track
$548 \text{ Hz}$ by the passenger and $458 \text{ Hz}$ by the person near the track
$500 \text{ Hz}$ by the passenger and $458 \text{ Hz}$ by the person near the track
questions.solution:
Velocity of the train, $v_s = 108 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 108 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 30 \text{ m/s}$

Velocity of the wind, $v_w = 36 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 36 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 10 \text{ m/s}$

For the passenger sitting in the train, the relative velocity between the source (train whistle) and the observer (passenger) is zero. Therefore, there is no Doppler shift, and the frequency heard by the passenger is equal to the actual frequency, which is $500 \text{ Hz}$.

For the person standing near the track whom the train has just passed, the train is moving away from the person. The sound travels from the train to the person, which is opposite to the direction of the wind (since the train is moving east and the wind is blowing east, the person is to the west of the train).

Effective speed of sound, $v_{eff} = v - v_w = 340 - 10 = 330 \text{ m/s}$

Since the source is moving away from the stationary observer, the apparent frequency $f'$ is given by:

$f' = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v_{eff}}{v_{eff} + v_s} \right)$

Substituting the values:

$f' = 500 \left( \dfrac{330}{330 + 30} \right)$

$f' = 500 \left( \dfrac{330}{360} \right) = 500 \times \dfrac{11}{12} \approx 458.33 \text{ Hz}$

Thus, the frequency heard by the person near the track is approximately $458 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: While riding a bicycle towards a vertical wall at $12 \text{ km h}^{-1}$, a boy whistles at his dog on the ground. Given that the whistle has a frequency of $1600 \text{ Hz}$ and the speed of sound in air is $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the frequency of the whistle as received by the wall.
questions.solution:
Speed of the source (boy on the bicycle), $v_s = 12 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 12 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = \dfrac{10}{3} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Frequency of the source, $f = 1600 \text{ Hz}$

Speed of sound in air, $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The wall acts as a stationary observer while the source is moving towards it. Using the Doppler effect formula for a moving source and a stationary observer, the apparent frequency $f'$ received by the wall is given by:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f' = 1600 \left( \dfrac{330}{330 - \dfrac{10}{3}} \right)$

$f' = 1600 \left( \dfrac{330}{\dfrac{990 - 10}{3}} \right)$

$f' = 1600 \left( \dfrac{990}{980} \right)$

$f' = 1600 \times \dfrac{99}{98}$

$f' \approx 1616.32 \text{ Hz}$

The closest frequency is $1616 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: While riding a bicycle towards a vertical wall at $12 \text{ km h}^{-1}$, a boy whistles at his dog on the ground. Given that the whistle has a frequency of $1600 \text{ Hz}$ and the speed of sound in air is $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the frequency of the reflected whistle as received by the boy.
questions.solution:
Speed of the boy, $v_{b} = 12 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 12 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = \dfrac{10}{3} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The boy acts as a source moving towards the stationary wall. The frequency of the sound reaching the wall is:

$f_{1} = f_{0} \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_{b}} \right)$

The wall reflects the sound with the same frequency $f_{1}$. Now, the boy acts as an observer moving towards the stationary wall. The frequency of the reflected sound received by the boy is:

$f_{2} = f_{1} \left( \dfrac{v + v_{b}}{v} \right) = f_{0} \left( \dfrac{v + v_{b}}{v - v_{b}} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f_{2} = 1600 \left( \dfrac{330 + \dfrac{10}{3}}{330 - \dfrac{10}{3}} \right)$

$f_{2} = 1600 \left( \dfrac{990 + 10}{990 - 10} \right) = 1600 \left( \dfrac{1000}{980} \right)$

$f_{2} = 1600 \times \dfrac{50}{49} = \dfrac{80000}{49} \approx 1632.65 \text{ Hz}$

The closest value among the options is $1632 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sound source is fixed at the origin and continuously emits sound at a frequency of $660 \text{ Hz}$. The sound propagates through air at a speed of $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. A listener travels along the line $x = 336 \text{ m}$ with a constant speed of $26 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the frequency of the sound observed by the listener when he is positioned at $y = 0$.
questions.solution:
The sound source is stationary and fixed at the origin $(0,0)$.

The listener travels along the line $x = 336 \text{ m}$, which means the listener's velocity is directed along the y-axis (i.e., $\vec{v}_L = \pm 26 \hat{j} \text{ m s}^{-1}$).

When the listener is positioned at $y = 0$, their coordinates are $(336, 0)$. The line of sight joining the source to the listener is along the x-axis.

The angle $\theta$ between the listener's velocity vector (along the y-axis) and the line of sight (along the x-axis) is $90^{\circ}$.

The component of the listener's velocity along the direction of sound propagation is:
$v_{L,\parallel} = v_L \cos(90^{\circ}) = 0$

According to the Doppler effect for a stationary source and a moving observer, the observed frequency $f'$ is given by:
$f' = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v \pm v_{L,\parallel}}{v} \right)$

Substituting the given values:
$f' = 660 \left( \dfrac{330 \pm 0}{330} \right) = 660 \text{ Hz}$

Since the listener's velocity has no component along the line joining the source and the listener at that instant, there is no Doppler shift. The observed frequency is equal to the emitted frequency.

Answer: $660 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person standing on a road transmits a sound signal to the driver of a car moving away from him at $72 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. The signal, travelling in air at $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ with a frequency of $1600 \text{ Hz}$, reflects off the body of the car and returns. Determine the frequency of the reflected signal heard by the person.
questions.solution:
Speed of the car, $v_c = 72 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 72 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Speed of sound, $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Original frequency, $f_0 = 1600 \text{ Hz}$

The frequency received by the car (acting as an observer moving away from the stationary source) is given by:

$f_1 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v - v_c}{v} \right)$

The car then reflects the sound, acting as a moving source moving away from the stationary person. The frequency heard by the person is:

$f_2 = f_1 \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_c} \right)$

Substituting $f_1$ into the equation for $f_2$:

$f_2 = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v - v_c}{v} \right) \left( \dfrac{v}{v + v_c} \right) = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v - v_c}{v + v_c} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f_2 = 1600 \left( \dfrac{330 - 20}{330 + 20} \right)$

$f_2 = 1600 \left( \dfrac{310}{350} \right) = 1600 \times \dfrac{31}{35}$

$f_2 = \dfrac{49600}{35} \approx 1417.14 \text{ Hz}$

Thus, the frequency of the reflected signal heard by the person is approximately $1417 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Travelling towards a cliff, a car moves with a speed of $54 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. The car's horn emits sound at a frequency of $400 \text{ Hz}$, and the speed of sound is $335 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Determine the wavelength of the sound emitted by the horn in the region in front of the car.
questions.solution:
Speed of the car, $v_s = 54 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 54 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Frequency of the horn, $f = 400 \text{ Hz}$

Speed of sound, $v = 335 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The wavelength of the sound in the region in front of the moving car is the apparent wavelength due to the source moving towards the observer. It is given by:

$\lambda' = \dfrac{v - v_s}{f}$

Substituting the given values:

$\lambda' = \dfrac{335 - 15}{400}$

$\lambda' = \dfrac{320}{400} \text{ m}$

$\lambda' = 0.8 \text{ m} = 80 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Travelling towards a cliff, a car moves with a speed of $54 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. The car's horn emits sound at a frequency of $400 \text{ Hz}$, and the speed of sound is $335 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the wavelength of the sound wave after it is reflected from the cliff.
questions.solution:
Speed of the car, $v_c = 54 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 54 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Frequency of the horn, $f_0 = 400 \text{ Hz}$

Speed of sound, $v = 335 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The apparent frequency of the sound reaching the cliff is given by the Doppler effect for a moving source and stationary observer:

$f' = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_c} \right)$

The cliff acts as a stationary source reflecting the sound at this frequency $f'$. The wavelength of the reflected sound wave is:

$\lambda' = \dfrac{v}{f'} = \dfrac{v - v_c}{f_0}$

Substituting the given values:

$\lambda' = \dfrac{335 - 15}{400}$

$\lambda' = \dfrac{320}{400} = 0.8 \text{ m}$

$\lambda' = 80 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Travelling towards a cliff, a car moves with a speed of $54 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. The car's horn emits sound at a frequency of $400 \text{ Hz}$, and the speed of sound is $335 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. What frequency does a person sitting inside the car hear for the reflected sound wave?
questions.solution:
Speed of the car, $v_c = 54 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 54 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Frequency of the horn, $f_0 = 400 \text{ Hz}$

Speed of sound, $v = 335 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The sound is reflected from the cliff. The cliff acts as a stationary observer for the incident sound and as a stationary source for the reflected sound.

The apparent frequency heard by the person in the car is given by the Doppler effect formula for a source and observer approaching each other:

$f' = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v + v_c}{v - v_c} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f' = 400 \left( \dfrac{335 + 15}{335 - 15} \right)$

$f' = 400 \left( \dfrac{350}{320} \right)$

$f' = 400 \times \dfrac{35}{32}$

$f' = 12.5 \times 35 = 437.5 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Travelling towards a cliff, a car moves with a speed of $54 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. The car's horn emits sound at a frequency of $400 \text{ Hz}$, and the speed of sound is $335 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. How many beats does a person in the car hear in $10$ seconds between the direct sound from the horn and the sound coming after reflection?
options: $0$ (the beat frequency is too high to be resolved)
questions.solution:
Speed of the car, $v_c = 54 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The frequency of the direct sound heard by the person in the car is the same as the original frequency, since there is no relative motion between the person and the horn:

$f_1 = 400 \text{ Hz}$

For the reflected sound, the car acts as a moving source approaching the stationary cliff, and the person in the car acts as a moving observer approaching the stationary cliff. The apparent frequency of the reflected sound heard by the person is:

$f_2 = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_c}{v - v_c} \right)$

Substituting the given values:

$f_2 = 400 \left( \dfrac{335 + 15}{335 - 15} \right) = 400 \left( \dfrac{350}{320} \right) = 437.5 \text{ Hz}$

The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies:

$f_b = f_2 - f_1 = 437.5 - 400 = 37.5 \text{ Hz}$

The number of beats heard in $10$ seconds is:

$n = f_b \times 10 = 37.5 \times 10 = 375$

questions.q: An operator seated in his base camp transmits a sound signal of frequency $400 \text{ Hz}$. The signal is reflected back by a car moving towards him. The frequency of the reflected sound is measured to be $410 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the speed of the car, given that the speed of sound in air is $324 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Let the speed of the car be $v_c$.

The car acts as a moving observer receiving the sound from the stationary base camp. The frequency received by the car is $f' = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_c}{v} \right)$.

The car then reflects the sound, acting as a moving source. The frequency received by the stationary base camp is $f'' = f' \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_c} \right)$.

Combining these, the apparent frequency of the reflected sound is $f'' = f \left( \dfrac{v + v_c}{v - v_c} \right)$.

Substituting the given values $f = 400 \text{ Hz}$, $f'' = 410 \text{ Hz}$, and $v = 324 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$410 = 400 \left( \dfrac{324 + v_c}{324 - v_c} \right)$

$\dfrac{41}{40} = \dfrac{324 + v_c}{324 - v_c}$

$41(324 - v_c) = 40(324 + v_c)$

$41 \times 324 - 41 v_c = 40 \times 324 + 40 v_c$

$324(41 - 40) = 81 v_c$

$324 = 81 v_c$

$v_c = 4 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.q: A source of sound moves along the X-axis at a speed of $22 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, continuously emitting a sound of frequency $2.0 \text{ kHz}$ that travels in air at a speed of $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. A listener $Q$ stands on the Y-axis at a distance of $330 \text{ m}$ from the origin. At $t = 0$, the source crosses the origin $P$. What will be the frequency heard by the listener at the instant the sound emitted from $P$ reaches them?
questions.solution:
The sound received by the listener was emitted when the source was at the origin $P$.

At this instant, the velocity of the source is directed along the X-axis, while the line joining the source to the listener lies along the Y-axis.

The angle $\theta$ between the velocity vector of the source and the line of sight from the source to the listener is $90^\circ$.

The apparent frequency $f'$ heard by the listener is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s \cos \theta} \right)$

where $v$ is the speed of sound and $v_s$ is the speed of the source.

Substituting $\theta = 90^\circ$, we get $\cos 90^\circ = 0$:

$f' = f \left( \dfrac{v}{v - 0} \right) = f$

Given the original frequency $f = 2.0 \text{ kHz}$, the frequency heard by the listener is:

$f' = 2.0 \text{ kHz}$

A listener $Q$ stands on the Y-axis at a distance of $330 \text{ m}$ from the origin. At $t = 0$, the source crosses the origin $P$. Determine the time at which the sound emitted from the source at $P$ reaches the listener $Q$.
questions.solution:
The sound is emitted when the source crosses the origin $P$. According to the given information, the source is at $P$ at time $t = 0$.

The distance between the origin $P$ and the listener $Q$ is $d = 330 \text{ m}$.

The speed of sound in air is $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Note that the speed of sound in a medium is independent of the speed of the source.

The time taken for the sound to travel from $P$ to $Q$ is given by:
$t = \dfrac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Speed of sound}}$

$t = \dfrac{330 \text{ m}}{330 \text{ m s}^{-1}} = 1 \text{ s}$

Since the sound was emitted at $t = 0$, it reaches the listener $Q$ at $t = 1 \text{ s}$.

A listener $Q$ stands on the Y-axis at a distance of $330 \text{ m}$ from the origin. At $t = 0$, the source crosses the origin $P$. Where will the source be located at the instant the sound emitted from $P$ reaches the listener?
questions.solution:
Given:
Speed of the source, $v_s = 22 \text{ m s}^{-1}$
Speed of sound, $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$
Distance of listener $Q$ from the origin $P$, $d = 330 \text{ m}$

The time taken by the sound to travel from the origin $P$ to the listener $Q$ is:

$x = v_s \times t = 22 \times 1 = 22 \text{ m}$

Therefore, the source will be located at $x = 22 \text{ m}$ when the sound emitted from $P$ reaches the listener.

questions.q: Travelling along the Y-axis with a speed of $22 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, a source emits sound at a frequency of $4000 \text{ Hz}$. A listener is located on the ground at the coordinates $(660 \text{ m}, 0)$. Determine the frequency of the sound detected by the listener at the exact moment the source crosses the origin. The speed of sound in air is $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Let the source cross the origin at $t = 0$. The sound detected by the listener at $t = 0$ was emitted by the source at an earlier time $t = -t_0$.

During the time interval $t_0$, the sound travels a distance $d = v t_0$, where $v$ is the speed of sound. At $t = -t_0$, the source was at a distance $y = v_s t_0$ from the origin along the Y-axis.

The distance from the source at the time of emission to the listener at $(660, 0)$ is $d = \sqrt{660^2 + y^2}$. Thus, we have $d = v t_0$.

The component of the source's velocity along the line of sight towards the listener is $v_s \cos \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the source's velocity and the direction to the listener. From the geometry of the setup, we have:

$\cos \theta = \dfrac{y}{d} = \dfrac{v_s t_0}{v t_0} = \dfrac{v_s}{v}$

The apparent frequency $f$ detected by the listener is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s \cos \theta} \right)$

Substituting $\cos \theta = \dfrac{v_s}{v}$ into the formula, we get:

$f = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - \dfrac{v_s^2}{v}} \right) = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v^2}{v^2 - v_s^2} \right)$

Given $f_0 = 4000 \text{ Hz}$, $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $v_s = 22 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, we can substitute these values:

$f = 4000 \left( \dfrac{330^2}{330^2 - 22^2} \right)$

Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $22^2$, we get:

$f = 4000 \left( \dfrac{15^2}{15^2 - 1^2} \right) = 4000 \left( \dfrac{225}{224} \right)$

$f \approx 4017.86 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the frequency detected by the listener is $4018 \text{ Hz}$.

Answer: $4018 \text{ Hz}$

questions.q: Travelling along a straight line at a speed of $170 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, a source of sound emits a $1200 \text{ Hz}$ note. A detector is located $200 \text{ m}$ away from the source's line of motion. Determine the frequency of the sound received by the detector at the exact instant the source reaches its closest point to the detector. Assume the velocity of sound in air to be $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Let the source move along the x-axis and the detector be at $(0, d)$.

The source reaches the closest point to the detector at $t = 0$. The sound received by the detector at this instant was emitted by the source at an earlier time $-t_0$.

At time $-t_0$, the position of the source was $(-v_s t_0, 0)$. The distance between the source at the time of emission and the detector is $D = \sqrt{(-v_s t_0)^2 + d^2}$.

The time taken for the sound to travel this distance is $t_0$, so $D = v t_0$.

From the geometry, the angle $\theta$ between the velocity of the source and the line of sight to the detector satisfies $\cos \theta = \dfrac{v_s t_0}{D} = \dfrac{v_s t_0}{v t_0} = \dfrac{v_s}{v}$.

The apparent frequency received by the detector is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f = f_0 \dfrac{v}{v - v_s \cos \theta}$

Substituting $\cos \theta = \dfrac{v_s}{v}$:

$f = f_0 \dfrac{v}{v - v_s \left(\dfrac{v_s}{v}\right)} = f_0 \dfrac{v^2}{v^2 - v_s^2}$

Given $v = 340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v_s = 170 \text{ m s}^{-1} = \dfrac{v}{2}$, and $f_0 = 1200 \text{ Hz}$:

$f = 1200 \times \dfrac{v^2}{v^2 - \left(\dfrac{v}{2}\right)^2} = 1200 \times \dfrac{1}{1 - \dfrac{1}{4}} = 1200 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 1600 \text{ Hz}$

questions.q: Travelling along a straight line at a speed of $170 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, a source of sound emits a $1200 \text{ Hz}$ note. A detector is located $200 \text{ m}$ away from the source's line of motion. Determine the distance separating the source and the detector at the instant the detector registers a frequency of $1200 \text{ Hz}$. Assume the velocity of sound in air to be $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The apparent frequency registered by the detector is given by the Doppler effect formula:

$f = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s \cos\theta} \right)$

where $v$ is the velocity of sound, $v_s$ is the velocity of the source, and $\theta$ is the angle between the source's velocity vector and the line joining the source to the detector at the instant the sound is emitted.

Given that the emitted frequency $f_0 = 1200 \text{ Hz}$ and the registered frequency $f = 1200 \text{ Hz}$, we have:

$1200 = 1200 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_s \cos\theta} \right)$

$\Rightarrow v - v_s \cos\theta = v$

$\Rightarrow \cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = 90^{\circ}$

This means the sound heard by the detector was emitted when the source was at the point of closest approach. At this instant, the distance between the source and the detector is $d = 200 \text{ m}$.

The time taken for this sound to reach the detector is:

$t = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{200}{340} = \dfrac{10}{17} \text{ s}$

During this time, the source continues to move forward. The distance traveled by the source in time $t$ is:

$x = v_s t = 170 \times \dfrac{10}{17} = 100 \text{ m}$

At the instant the detector registers the frequency, the source has moved $100 \text{ m}$ from the point of closest approach. The distance $D$ separating the source and the detector at this instant is:

$D = \sqrt{x^2 + d^2} = \sqrt{100^2 + 200^2}$

$D = \sqrt{10000 + 40000} = \sqrt{50000} = 100\sqrt{5} \text{ m}$

Using $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236$, we get:

$D \approx 100 \times 2.236 = 223.6 \text{ m}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the distance is $224 \text{ m}$.

questions.q: A small source of sound $S$ having a frequency of $500 \text{ Hz}$ is tied to the end of a light string and whirled in a vertical circle of radius $1.6 \text{ m}$. The string just remains tight when the source reaches the highest point. An observer is located at a large distance vertically above the centre of the circle. Determine the frequencies heard by the observer corresponding to the sound emitted by the source when it is at the exact same height as the centre. Assume the speed of sound in air is $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
For the string to just remain tight at the highest point, the tension must be zero. The centripetal force is provided entirely by gravity:

$\dfrac{mv_{top}^2}{R} = mg \Rightarrow v_{top} = \sqrt{gR}$

Using the conservation of mechanical energy, we can find the velocity of the source at the lowest point of the circular path:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv_{bot}^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{top}^2 + mg(2R)$

$v_{bot} = \sqrt{v_{top}^2 + 4gR} = \sqrt{gR + 4gR} = \sqrt{5gR}$

Substituting the given values $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $R = 1.6 \text{ m}$:

$v_{bot} = \sqrt{5 \times 10 \times 1.6} = \sqrt{80} \approx 8.94 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

From the given figure, the source is moving in a counterclockwise direction. The observer is at a large distance at the same height as the centre of the circle, so the line of sight is horizontal. The maximum frequency is heard when the source has the maximum velocity component directed towards the observer. This occurs at the lowest point of the circle, where the velocity is purely horizontal and directed towards the observer.

Using the Doppler effect formula for maximum frequency:

$f_{max} = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v}{v - v_{s,max}} \right)$

Substituting $f_0 = 500 \text{ Hz}$, $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $v_{s,max} = v_{bot} = \sqrt{80} \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$f_{max} = 500 \left( \dfrac{330}{330 - 8.94} \right)$

$f_{max} = 500 \left( \dfrac{330}{321.06} \right) \approx 513.9 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the maximum frequency heard by the observer is $514 \text{ Hz}$.

Answer: $514 \text{ Hz}$

questions.q: A small source of sound $S$ having a frequency of $500 \text{ Hz}$ is tied to the end of a light string and whirled in a vertical circle of radius $1.6 \text{ m}$. The string just remains tight when the source reaches the highest point. An observer is located at a large distance vertically above the centre of the circle. Determine the frequencies heard by the observer corresponding to the sound emitted by the source when it is at the exact same height as the centre. Assume the speed of sound in air is $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
At the highest point, the string just remains tight, so the tension is zero. The centripetal force is provided entirely by gravity:

$\dfrac{m v_{top}^2}{R} = m g \Rightarrow v_{top} = \sqrt{g R}$

Using conservation of mechanical energy between the highest point and the point at the same height as the centre:

$\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_{top}^2 + m g R$

$\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m (g R) + m g R = \dfrac{3}{2} m g R$

$v = \sqrt{3 g R}$

Substituting $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $R = 1.6 \text{ m}$:

$v = \sqrt{3 \times 10 \times 1.6} = \sqrt{48} \approx 6.93 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

When the source is at the same height as the centre, its velocity is directed vertically. Since the observer is at a large distance vertically above the centre, the velocity of the source is directly towards or away from the observer.

The maximum frequency heard (when the source moves upwards, towards the observer) is:

$f_{max} = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v_0}{v_0 - v} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{330}{330 - 6.93} \right) \approx 510.7 \text{ Hz} \approx 511 \text{ Hz}$

The minimum frequency heard (when the source moves downwards, away from the observer) is:

$f_{min} = f_0 \left( \dfrac{v_0}{v_0 + v} \right) = 500 \left( \dfrac{330}{330 + 6.93} \right) \approx 489.7 \text{ Hz} \approx 490 \text{ Hz}$

Answer: $490 \text{ Hz}$ and $511 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Placed at a large distance from an observer, a source emits a sound of frequency $\nu$. The source begins traveling towards the observer with a uniform acceleration $a$. Determine the frequency heard by the observer corresponding to the wave emitted just after the source starts. The speed of sound in the medium is given as $v$.
questions.solution:
The time period of the emitted sound is $T = \dfrac{1}{ u}$.

Let the source emit the first wave crest at $t = 0$. The position of this crest at time $t$ is $x_1 = vt$.

The second wave crest is emitted at $t = T$. During this time, the source moves a distance $x_s = \dfrac{1}{2}aT^2$.

The position of the second crest at time $t$ (where $t > T$) is $x_2 = x_s + v(t - T) = \dfrac{1}{2}aT^2 + v(t - T)$.

The apparent wavelength $\lambda'$ is the distance between the first and second crests:

$\lambda' = x_1 - x_2 = vt - \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}aT^2 + v(t - T) ight] = vT - \dfrac{1}{2}aT^2$

The frequency $ u'$ heard by the observer is given by $ u' = \dfrac{v}{\lambda'}$.

Substituting $T = \dfrac{1}{ u}$ into the expression for $\lambda'$:

$ u' = \dfrac{v}{\dfrac{v}{ u} - \dfrac{a}{2 u^2}}$

$ u' = \dfrac{2v u^2}{2v u - a}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When the air inside a closed pipe is at a temperature of $20^\circ \text{C}$, its fundamental frequency is $293 \text{ Hz}$. Determine its fundamental frequency if the temperature changes to $22^\circ \text{C}$.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a closed pipe is given by $f = \dfrac{v}{4L}$.

The speed of sound in a gas is proportional to the square root of its absolute temperature, $v \propto \sqrt{T}$.

Therefore, the fundamental frequency is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature, $f \propto \sqrt{T}$.

Given $T_1 = 20^{\circ}\text{C} = 293\text{ K}$ and $f_1 = 293\text{ Hz}$.

The new temperature is $T_2 = 22^{\circ}\text{C} = 295\text{ K}$.

Using the relation $\dfrac{f_2}{f_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}$:

$f_2 = 293 \sqrt{\dfrac{295}{293}} = \sqrt{293 \times 295}$

$f_2 = \sqrt{(294 - 1)(294 + 1)} = \sqrt{294^2 - 1}$

$f_2 \approx 294\text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A Kundt's tube apparatus features a copper rod of length $1.0 \text{ m}$ clamped at $25 \text{ cm}$ from one of its ends. The tube is filled with air having a sound speed of $340 \text{ m/s}$. The powder gathers in heaps separated by a distance of $5.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the speed of sound waves in copper.
questions.solution:
The distance between the heaps of powder in a Kundt's tube corresponds to the distance between two consecutive nodes in the air column, which is $\dfrac{\lambda_a}{2}$.

$\dfrac{\lambda_a}{2} = 5.0 \text{ cm} \Rightarrow \lambda_a = 10.0 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$

The frequency of the sound wave is given by:

$f = \dfrac{v_a}{\lambda_a} = \dfrac{340}{0.1} = 3400 \text{ Hz}$

The copper rod of length $1.0 \text{ m}$ is clamped at $25 \text{ cm}$ from one end. The clamped point acts as a node and the free ends act as antinodes. The distance from the node to the nearest antinode is $\dfrac{\lambda_c}{4}$.

$\dfrac{\lambda_c}{4} = 25 \text{ cm} \Rightarrow \lambda_c = 100 \text{ cm} = 1.0 \text{ m}$

The speed of sound in the copper rod is:

$v_c = f \lambda_c = 3400 \times 1.0 = 3400 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a Kundt's tube apparatus, a steel rod of length $1.0 \text{ m}$ is clamped at its centre. It is set into vibration in its fundamental mode with a frequency of $2600 \text{ Hz}$. The lycopodium powder dispersed inside the tube gathers into heaps that are separated by $6.5 \text{ cm}$. Determine the speed of sound in steel and in air, respectively.
questions.solution:
For the steel rod clamped at the centre and vibrating in its fundamental mode, the centre is a node and the ends are antinodes.

Length of the rod, $L = \dfrac{\lambda_{\text{steel}}}{2}$

$\lambda_{\text{steel}} = 2L = 2 \times 1.0 = 2.0 \text{ m}$

Speed of sound in steel, $v_{\text{steel}} = f \lambda_{\text{steel}} = 2600 \times 2.0 = 5200 \text{ m/s}$

In the Kundt's tube, the distance between consecutive heaps of lycopodium powder represents the distance between consecutive nodes of the standing wave in air.

$\dfrac{\lambda_{\text{air}}}{2} = 6.5 \text{ cm} = 0.065 \text{ m}$

$\lambda_{\text{air}} = 2 \times 0.065 = 0.13 \text{ m}$

Speed of sound in air, $v_{\text{air}} = f \lambda_{\text{air}} = 2600 \times 0.13 = 338 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sound source with an adjustable frequency generates $2$ beats per second with a tuning fork when its frequency is set to either $476 \text{ Hz}$ or $480 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the frequency of the tuning fork.
questions.solution:
Let the frequency of the tuning fork be $f$.

The beat frequency is the absolute difference between the frequencies of the two sound sources.

Given that the beat frequency is $2 \text{ Hz}$ when the source frequency is $476 \text{ Hz}$:

$|f - 476| = 2 \Rightarrow f = 474 \text{ Hz} \text{ or } 478 \text{ Hz}$

Also, the beat frequency is $2 \text{ Hz}$ when the source frequency is $480 \text{ Hz}$:

$|f - 480| = 2 \Rightarrow f = 478 \text{ Hz} \text{ or } 482 \text{ Hz}$

The common value satisfying both conditions is $f = 478 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tuning fork generates $4$ beats per second when sounded with another tuning fork having a frequency of $256 \text{ Hz}$. When the first tuning fork is loaded with a small amount of wax, the beat frequency increases to $6$ per second. Determine the original frequency of the first tuning fork.
questions.solution:
Let the frequency of the first tuning fork be $n_1$ and the second be $n_2 = 256 \text{ Hz}$.

The initial beat frequency is $4 \text{ Hz}$.

$n_1 = n_2 \pm 4 = 256 \pm 4$

$n_1 = 260 \text{ Hz}$ or $252 \text{ Hz}$

When the first tuning fork is loaded with wax, its frequency decreases.

If $n_1 = 260 \text{ Hz}$, a small decrease in frequency would initially decrease the beat frequency (for example, to $259 \text{ Hz}$, giving $3$ beats).

If $n_1 = 252 \text{ Hz}$, a small decrease in frequency would increase the beat frequency (for example, to $250 \text{ Hz}$, giving $6$ beats).

Since the beat frequency increases to $6 \text{ Hz}$, the original frequency of the first tuning fork must be $252 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the frequency of beats produced in air when two sources of sound are activated, with one emitting a wavelength of $32 \text{ cm}$ and the other a wavelength of $32.2 \text{ cm}$. The speed of sound in air is $350 \text{ m/s}$.
questions.solution:
Given:

Speed of sound, $v = 350 \text{ m/s}$

Wavelength of first source, $\lambda_1 = 32 \text{ cm} = 0.32 \text{ m}$

Wavelength of second source, $\lambda_2 = 32.2 \text{ cm} = 0.322 \text{ m}$

The frequencies of the sound produced by the two sources are:

$f_1 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{350}{0.32} = 1093.75 \text{ Hz}$

$f_2 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{350}{0.322} \approx 1086.96 \text{ Hz}$

The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies:

$f_{beat} = f_1 - f_2 = 1093.75 - 1086.96 = 6.79 \text{ Hz}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the beat frequency is approximately $7 \text{ Hz}$.
